paragraphs: A direct object answers whom or what without a preposition. With `avoir`, French agrees the participle only when that object has already appeared, which happens in three situations: after the object pronouns `le`, `la`, `les`, `me`, `te`, `nous`, `vous`; after the relative pronoun `que`; and in a question introduced by `quel` or `combien de`. In `Nous les avons envoyées`, `les` stands for `les demandes`, so the participle takes `-es`.

With `être` and a non-reflexive verb, agreement is with the subject and requires no analysis. Reflexive verbs need one extra step: decide what the reflexive pronoun stands for. In `elles se sont lavées`, `se` is the direct object, so the participle agrees. In `elles se sont lavé les mains`, the direct object is `les mains`, placed after the verb, and `se` is indirect, so there is no agreement. The same logic explains `elles se sont parlé`, where `parler à` makes `se` indirect.
points: Identify the auxiliary before looking for anything else.
With `avoir`, search to the left of the participle for a direct object.
Agree with a preceding `le`, `la`, `les`, or with the relative `que`.
With non-reflexive `être`, agree with the subject.
With a reflexive verb, agree only when the reflexive pronoun is the direct object.

examples.french: Les demandes ? Nous les avons envoyées hier après-midi.
examples.english: The applications? We sent them yesterday afternoon.
examples.note: The preceding direct object « les » is feminine plural.

examples.french: La lettre que j’ai écrite est restée sans réponse.
examples.english: The letter that I wrote went unanswered.
examples.note: The relative « que » is the preceding direct object.

examples.french: Les formulaires que nous avons remplis sont maintenant complets.
examples.english: The forms that we filled in are now complete.
examples.note: Masculine plural agreement after « que ».

examples.french: Elle s’est lavé les mains avant le rendez-vous.
examples.english: She washed her hands before the appointment.
examples.note: The direct object « les mains » follows, so no agreement.

examples.french: Les deux conseillères se sont parlé avant la réunion.
examples.english: The two advisers spoke to each other before the meeting.
examples.note: « Parler à » makes « se » indirect, so the participle does not agree.

mistakes.avoid: Les documents ? Elle les a envoyé hier.
mistakes.prefer: Les documents ? Elle les a envoyés hier.
mistakes.why: `Les` stands for the masculine plural `les documents` and precedes the participle.

mistakes.avoid: Elles se sont lavées les mains avant de partir.
mistakes.prefer: Elles se sont lavé les mains avant de partir.
mistakes.why: The direct object is `les mains`, which follows the verb; `se` is indirect.

vocabulary.example: Les formulaires que nous avons remplis étaient en double exemplaire.
vocabulary.note: Regular `-ir` verb of the `finir` type; participle `rempli`.

vocabulary.example: La lettre que j’ai écrite est partie ce matin.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; triggers a feminine singular participle when placed before.

vocabulary.example: Les pièces justificatives que j’ai jointes figurent en annexe.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun, usually plural in administrative language.

vocabulary.example: Une annexe détaillée accompagne le rapport final.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; `en annexe` means attached.

practice.prompt: Agree if required: « Les attestations que j’ai (recevoir) », « Elle s’est (couper) le doigt », « Elles sont (partir) ».
practice.hint: One preceding direct object, one following direct object, one subject agreement.
practice.answer: Les attestations que j’ai reçues, Elle s’est coupé le doigt, Elles sont parties

takeaways: `Avoir` agrees only with a direct object placed before the participle.
Non-reflexive `être` agrees with the subject, automatically.
A reflexive pronoun agrees only when it is itself the direct object.
keywords: past-participle agreement with a preceding object

lessons.title: L’imparfait
lessons.summary: The imperfect describes a past situation from the inside: background, description, a state, an action in progress, or a repeated habit. Build it from the present `nous` form minus `-ons`, then add `-ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient`. `Être` is the only verb with an irregular stem, `ét-`. Verbs in `-cer` write `ç` and verbs in `-ger` keep `e` before endings starting with `a`: `je commençais`, `il neigeait`.
objectives: Derive the imperfect stem from the present `nous` form.
Choose the imperfect for habit, description, and ongoing background.
Apply the spelling adjustments of `-cer` and `-ger` verbs.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: The imperfect presents a past situation without marking its beginning or end. It therefore covers four everyday uses: a repeated habit (`je faisais du bénévolat chaque semaine`), a description or state (`il faisait froid`), an action in progress interrupted by another (`je travaillais quand la connexion est tombée`), and a past viewpoint in reported speech (`il a dit qu’il voulait déménager`).

The formation is unusually regular. Take the present `nous` form, remove `-ons`, and add the endings: `nous finissons` gives `je finissais`, `nous prenons` gives `je prenais`, `nous faisons` gives `je faisais`. Only `être` escapes this, using `ét-`. Two spelling families protect pronunciation: `-cer` verbs write `ç` before `a` (`je commençais` but `nous commencions`), and `-ger` verbs keep the `e` (`il neigeait`, `je mangeais`, but `nous mangions`).
points: Start from the present `nous` form, not from the infinitive.
Use the imperfect for a habit, a description, or an action in progress.
Remember the single irregular stem: `ét-` for `être`.
Write `ç` in `-cer` verbs before `-ais`, `-ait`, `-aient`.
Keep the `e` in `-ger` verbs before those same endings.

examples.french: Je travaillais à distance lorsque la connexion est tombée en panne.
examples.english: I was working remotely when the connection went down.
examples.note: Imperfect for the ongoing action, compound past for the interruption.

examples.french: Quand j’étais étudiant, je faisais du bénévolat chaque semaine.
examples.english: When I was a student, I volunteered every week.
examples.note: Irregular stem ét- and a repeated habit.

examples.french: Il faisait froid et les routes étaient glissantes ce matin-là.
examples.english: It was cold and the roads were slippery that morning.
examples.note: Description and background.

examples.french: Je commençais mon bénévolat et il neigeait déjà sur la ville.
examples.english: I was beginning my volunteer work and it was already snowing over the city.
examples.note: `-cer` takes ç and `-ger` keeps e before -ait.

examples.french: Nous commencions toujours la réunion par un tour de table.
examples.english: We always started the meeting with a round of introductions.
examples.note: No ç before -ions, because the ending does not start with a.

mistakes.avoid: Quand j’étais petit, j’ai nagé chaque matin.
mistakes.prefer: Quand j’étais petit, je nageais chaque matin.
mistakes.why: A repeated childhood habit takes the imperfect, not the compound past.

mistakes.avoid: Je commencais mon stage en septembre.
mistakes.prefer: Je commençais mon stage en septembre.
mistakes.why: A `-cer` verb needs the cedilla before an ending starting with `a`.

vocabulary.example: Je faisais du bénévolat dans une banque alimentaire chaque samedi.
vocabulary.note: Fixed expression; `un bénévole` is the person.

vocabulary.example: Je commençais toujours par relire la consigne.
vocabulary.note: `-cer` verb: cedilla before `a` and `o`.

vocabulary.example: Une habitude quotidienne rend les progrès plus réguliers.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; `avoir l’habitude de` means to be used to.

vocabulary.example: Une connexion instable a interrompu l’entrevue en ligne.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; the ending -ion is a feminine hint.

practice.prompt: Put into the imperfect for `je` and `nous`: `manger`, `placer`, `être`.
practice.hint: The `nous` forms lose the spelling adjustment.
practice.answer: je mangeais / nous mangions, je plaçais / nous placions, j’étais / nous étions

takeaways: Stem from the present `nous` form; only `être` is irregular.
Habit, description, ongoing action, past viewpoint.
`ç` and `e` appear only before endings starting with `a`.

lessons.title: Le choix d’un temps du passé
lessons.summary: Use the compound past for a bounded, completed event and the imperfect for the surrounding description or habit. Add the pluperfect for an event completed before another past event: it is formed with the imperfect of `avoir` or `être` plus a past participle (`j’avais déposé`, `elle était partie`). The simple past (`il entra`) belongs to literary and historical writing; recognise it when reading, but use the compound past yourself.
objectives: Separate narrative events from background information.
Form and place the pluperfect for an earlier past event.
Recognise simple-past forms without producing them.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: A narrative has two planes. Events that advance the story are bounded and take the compound past. Description, states, weather, feelings, and repeated habits form the background and take the imperfect. A single sentence often contains both: `Je préparais mon entrevue` sets the scene, `quand la responsable m’a appelé` moves the story forward.

A third tense is needed as soon as one past event happens before another. The pluperfect, `le plus-que-parfait`, is built with the imperfect of the auxiliary plus the past participle, and it follows the same auxiliary and agreement rules as the compound past: `j’avais déposé ma demande`, `elle était déjà partie`, `nous nous étions inscrits`. It is also the tense used after `si` for an unreal past condition. The simple past, `le passé simple`, replaces the compound past in literary narration; forms such as `il entra`, `elle fut`, `ils prirent` are for recognition only.
points: Ask whether the verb advances the story or paints the scene.
Use the compound past for the event and the imperfect for the setting.
Use the pluperfect for whatever happened before the main past event.
Build the pluperfect with the imperfect of `avoir` or `être` plus a participle.
Recognise `il entra` or `elle fut` as literary narration, not as everyday speech.

examples.french: Je préparais mon entrevue quand la responsable m’a appelé.
examples.english: I was preparing for my interview when the manager called me.
examples.note: Background in the imperfect, event in the compound past.

examples.french: J’ai déménagé au Québec il y a quelques semaines.
examples.english: I moved to Quebec a few weeks ago.
examples.note: A single bounded event.

examples.french: Quand je suis arrivé au guichet, j’avais déjà rempli le formulaire en ligne.
examples.english: When I arrived at the counter, I had already completed the form online.
examples.note: Pluperfect for the action completed before the main past event.

examples.french: Elle était partie avant que la décision soit annoncée.
examples.english: She had left before the decision was announced.
examples.note: Pluperfect with the auxiliary être and subject agreement.

examples.french: Il entra dans la salle, salua l’assemblée et s’assit.
examples.english: He entered the room, greeted the assembly, and sat down.
examples.note: Simple past: recognise it in written narration.

mistakes.avoid: Quand je suis arrivé, j’ai déjà envoyé le dossier la veille.
mistakes.prefer: Quand je suis arrivé, j’avais déjà envoyé le dossier la veille.
mistakes.why: An action completed before another past action requires the pluperfect.

mistakes.avoid: Hier, il faisait la demande et il a obtenu une réponse immédiate.
mistakes.prefer: Hier, il a fait la demande et il a obtenu une réponse immédiate.
mistakes.why: Both verbs are bounded events, so both take the compound past.

vocabulary.example: Nous avions déménagé deux fois avant de trouver ce logement.
vocabulary.note: `-ger` verb; keeps the `e` before `a` and `o`.

vocabulary.example: J’avais déposé ma demande avant la date limite.
vocabulary.note: Regular `-er` verb; `déposer un dossier` is standard administrative usage.

vocabulary.example: Une entrevue d’embauche m’attendait le lendemain matin.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun used in Canada; `un entretien` in France.

vocabulary.example: Un guichet unique regroupe désormais toutes les démarches.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; `un guichet automatique` is a cash machine.

practice.prompt: Complete with the right past tense: « Quand elle (arriver) à la réunion, tout le monde (partir) déjà. »
practice.hint: The second verb happened before the first.
practice.answer: Quand elle est arrivée à la réunion, tout le monde était déjà parti.

takeaways: Event equals compound past; scene equals imperfect.
Earlier than the past equals pluperfect: imperfect auxiliary plus participle.
The simple past is for reading, not for producing.
keywords: choosing a past tense and the pluperfect

lessons.title: Les formes du futur
lessons.summary: The simple future adds `-ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont` to the infinitive, dropping the final `e` of an `-re` infinitive. Frequent irregular stems must be memorised: `être` gives `ser-`, `avoir` gives `aur-`, `faire` gives `fer-`, `aller` gives `ir-`, `venir` gives `viendr-`, `pouvoir` gives `pourr-`, `vouloir` gives `voudr-`, `voir` gives `verr-`, `devoir` gives `devr-`. The near future uses present `aller` plus an infinitive, and the negative wraps the conjugated `aller`.
objectives: Build the simple future from a regular or irregular stem.
Choose between the simple future and the near future.
Use the future after time conjunctions where English uses the present.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: The simple future is a single word: infinitive plus ending. `Parler` gives `je parlerai`, `finir` gives `je finirai`, and `attendre` drops its `e` to give `j’attendrai`. The endings are the present forms of `avoir` reduced, which is why every simple future ends in `-ai`, `-as`, `-a`, `-ons`, `-ez`, `-ont`. Irregular verbs change only the stem, never the endings.

The near future, `aller` plus infinitive, presents an action as planned or imminent and is very common in speech: `Nous allons présenter notre projet demain`. In the negative, only the conjugated `aller` is surrounded: `La ville ne va pas construire de logements`. One difference from English is decisive in writing: after `quand`, `lorsque`, `dès que`, and `aussitôt que`, French uses the future when the action is future, where English uses the present.
points: Add the endings straight to the infinitive for regular verbs.
Drop the final `e` of an `-re` infinitive before adding the ending.
Memorise the nine frequent irregular stems as a block.
Wrap only the conjugated `aller` when negating the near future.
Use the future, not the present, after `quand`, `lorsque`, and `dès que`.

examples.french: Nous réduirons nos déchets grâce à ce nouveau programme municipal.
examples.english: We will reduce our waste thanks to this new municipal program.
examples.note: Regular formation on an -re infinitive.

examples.french: Nous serons prêts et nous aurons tous les documents demandés.
examples.english: We will be ready and we will have all the requested documents.
examples.note: Irregular stems ser- and aur-.

examples.french: Je prendrai rendez-vous dès que le bureau ouvrira.
examples.english: I will make an appointment as soon as the office opens.
examples.note: French uses the future in both clauses after « dès que ».

examples.french: Nous allons présenter notre projet devant le comité demain.
examples.english: We are going to present our project to the committee tomorrow.
examples.note: Near future for a planned action.

examples.french: La ville ne va pas construire de logements sur ce terrain.
examples.english: The city is not going to build housing on this land.
examples.note: The negative surrounds « va », and « des » becomes « de ».

mistakes.avoid: Quand j’arrive au Canada, je chercherai un emploi.
mistakes.prefer: Quand j’arriverai au Canada, je chercherai un emploi.
mistakes.why: After `quand`, French uses the future for a future action, unlike English.

mistakes.avoid: Il ne va pas venir pas à la réunion.
mistakes.prefer: Il ne va pas venir à la réunion.
mistakes.why: In the near future the negative surrounds only the conjugated `aller`.

vocabulary.example: Nous réduirons la consommation d’énergie de vingt pour cent.
vocabulary.note: `-re` verb; the future drops the final `e`: `je réduirai`.

vocabulary.example: Vous pourrez suivre votre demande en ligne dès lundi.
vocabulary.note: Irregular future stem `pourr-`.

vocabulary.example: Un déchet mal trié complique tout le processus de recyclage.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun, usually used in the plural: `les déchets`.

vocabulary.example: Un terrain municipal sera transformé en parc de quartier.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; also means ground or field.

practice.prompt: Put into the simple future: « Je (faire) la demande dès que je (pouvoir). »
practice.hint: Both verbs have irregular stems, and French keeps the future after `dès que`.
practice.answer: Je ferai la demande dès que je pourrai.

takeaways: Infinitive plus `-ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont`, with `-re` losing its `e`.
Nine irregular stems cover most of what you will need.
`Quand` plus future in French, where English uses the present.

lessons.title: Le conditionnel et les phrases avec « si »
lessons.summary: The present conditional uses the future stem with imperfect endings: `je postulerais`, `nous serions`. The past conditional uses the conditional of `avoir` or `être` plus a participle. Three condition patterns must be kept apart: `si` plus present with a future or imperative result; `si` plus imperfect with a present conditional; `si` plus pluperfect with a past conditional. Never place a future or a conditional directly after conditional `si`.
objectives: Form the present and past conditional from the future stem.
Match each type of condition to its pair of tenses.
Use the conditional alone for politeness and unconfirmed information.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: The conditional is built on the future stem, so any verb you can put in the future you can put in the conditional: `je serai` gives `je serais`, `il faudra` gives `il faudrait`. The endings are those of the imperfect. The past conditional adds a participle to a conditional auxiliary: `je serais parti`, `j’aurais postulé`.

Conditional sentences come in three fixed pairs. A real possibility uses `si` plus present, with a present, future, or imperative result: `Si vous avez des questions, appelez le service`. A hypothesis about now or later uses `si` plus imperfect with the present conditional: `Si j’avais plus d’expérience, je postulerais`. A counterfactual past uses `si` plus pluperfect with the past conditional: `Si j’avais connu ce programme, je me serais inscrit plus tôt`. Outside `si` clauses, the conditional alone softens a request (`Je voudrais un rendez-vous`) or marks unverified information (`Le service fermerait plus tôt`).
points: Take the future stem and add `-ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient`.
Keep the present after `si` when the condition is realistic.
Use the imperfect after `si` for a present or future hypothesis.
Use the pluperfect after `si` for a past that did not happen.
Use `je voudrais`, `pourriez-vous`, `j’aimerais` for polite requests.

examples.french: Si la ville améliore le service, davantage de résidents prendront le bus.
examples.english: If the city improves the service, more residents will take the bus.
examples.note: Real possibility: present plus future.

examples.french: Si vous avez des questions, appelez le service d’aide aux nouveaux arrivants.
examples.english: If you have questions, call the newcomer support service.
examples.note: Present plus imperative.

examples.french: Si j’avais plus d’expérience, je postulerais à ce poste.
examples.english: If I had more experience, I would apply for this position.
examples.note: Present hypothesis: imperfect plus present conditional.

examples.french: Si j’avais connu ce programme, je me serais inscrit plus tôt.
examples.english: If I had known about this program, I would have enrolled earlier.
examples.note: Past counterfactual: pluperfect plus past conditional.

examples.french: Je voudrais prendre rendez-vous avec une conseillère en emploi.
examples.english: I would like to make an appointment with an employment adviser.
examples.note: Conditional alone for a polite request.

mistakes.avoid: Si tu travaillerais, tu réussirais l’examen.
mistakes.prefer: Si tu travaillais, tu réussirais l’examen.
mistakes.why: The conditional never follows `si` directly; the condition takes the imperfect.

mistakes.avoid: Si j’aurais su, je serais venu plus tôt.
mistakes.prefer: Si j’avais su, je serais venu plus tôt.
mistakes.why: A past counterfactual requires the pluperfect after `si`.

vocabulary.example: Si la ville améliorait le service, davantage de résidents prendraient le bus.
vocabulary.note: Regular `-er` verb; the conditional stem is the full infinitive.

vocabulary.example: Je voudrais obtenir une attestation de résidence.
vocabulary.note: Conditional `je voudrais` is the standard polite request form.

vocabulary.example: Un délai de traitement plus court serait apprécié par tous les usagers.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun phrase; the gender comes from `délai`.

vocabulary.example: Une hypothèse raisonnable mérite d’être vérifiée avant la conclusion.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun beginning with a mute h.

practice.prompt: Complete: « Si le service (être) ouvert samedi, je (déposer) mon dossier ce week-end. »
practice.hint: This is a hypothesis about the present, not a real possibility.
practice.answer: Si le service était ouvert samedi, je déposerais mon dossier ce week-end.

takeaways: Future stem plus imperfect endings equals the conditional.
Present with future, imperfect with present conditional, pluperfect with past conditional.
`Si` is never followed by a future or a conditional.

lessons.title: Le subjonctif présent
lessons.summary: The subjunctive is a mood used in a `que` clause after a trigger expressing will, emotion, doubt, necessity, judgement, or purpose. Form it from the present `ils` form minus `-ent`, plus `-e, -es, -e, -ions, -iez, -ent`. Memorise `être`, `avoir`, `aller`, `faire`, `pouvoir`, `savoir`. Use an infinitive when the two subjects are the same and `que` plus subjunctive when they differ. `Après que` takes the indicative in careful standard French.
objectives: Recognise the trigger that requires a subjunctive.
Form regular and frequent irregular subjunctives.
Decide between an infinitive and a `que` clause.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: A mood expresses how the speaker frames an event, not when it happens. The indicative presents an event as a fact; the subjunctive presents it as wanted, feared, doubted, required, judged, or aimed at. It therefore appears in a subordinate clause introduced by `que`, after a trigger in the main clause: `il faut que`, `je veux que`, `je doute que`, `je suis content que`, `il est important que`, `pour que`, `afin que`, `bien que`, `avant que`, `à condition que`, `jusqu’à ce que`.

Formation is regular for most verbs: take the present `ils` form, remove `-ent`, and add the subjunctive endings, so `ils réduisent` gives `que je réduise` and `que nous réduisions`. Six verbs are irregular and worth memorising in full: `sois/soyons`, `aie/ayons`, `aille/allions`, `fasse/fassions`, `puisse/puissions`, `sache/sachions`. The subject test decides the structure: same subject means an infinitive (`Je pars pour travailler`), different subjects mean `que` plus subjunctive (`Je pars pour que tu travailles`). One frequent trap: although `avant que` takes the subjunctive, `après que` takes the indicative in careful writing.
points: Look for the trigger in the main clause before choosing the mood.
Build the stem from the present `ils` form minus `-ent`.
Learn the six irregular verbs as complete paradigms.
Use an infinitive when the subject does not change.
Keep the indicative after `après que`.

examples.french: Il faut que nous réduisions la pollution dans les centres urbains.
examples.english: We must reduce pollution in urban centres.
examples.note: Regular formation from « ils réduisent ».

examples.french: Je suis heureuse que ma candidature ait été retenue.
examples.english: I am glad that my application was accepted.
examples.note: Emotion trigger with the irregular subjunctive of avoir.

examples.french: Je vous écris pour que vous connaissiez ma situation actuelle.
examples.english: I am writing so that you are aware of my current situation.
examples.note: Purpose with two different subjects.

examples.french: Je vous écris pour expliquer ma situation actuelle.
examples.english: I am writing to explain my current situation.
examples.note: Same subject, so an infinitive replaces the que clause.

examples.french: Bien que le dossier soit complet, il faut encore attendre la décision.
examples.english: Although the file is complete, we still have to wait for the decision.
examples.note: « Bien que » always takes the subjunctive.

mistakes.avoid: Après qu’il soit parti, nous avons commencé la réunion.
mistakes.prefer: Après qu’il est parti, nous avons commencé la réunion.
mistakes.why: In careful standard French, `après que` introduces a fact and takes the indicative.

mistakes.avoid: Je veux que je parte plus tôt aujourd’hui.
mistakes.prefer: Je veux partir plus tôt aujourd’hui.
mistakes.why: When the two subjects are identical, French uses an infinitive rather than a `que` clause.

vocabulary.example: Il faut que vous fournissiez une preuve de résidence.
vocabulary.note: Impersonal verb, used only with `il`; followed by an infinitive or by `que` plus subjunctive.

vocabulary.example: Il faut que j’aille au bureau des permis avant midi.
vocabulary.note: Irregular subjunctive: `que j’aille`, `que nous allions`.

vocabulary.example: Nous devons décider avant que le délai expire.
vocabulary.note: Takes the subjunctive, unlike `après que`, which takes the indicative.

vocabulary.example: Une décision favorable a été communiquée par courriel.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; the ending -sion is a feminine hint.

practice.prompt: Choose the mood: « Je reste jusqu’à ce que le guichet (fermer). » and « Après que le guichet (fermer), je suis rentré. »
practice.hint: One conjunction takes the subjunctive, the other the indicative.
practice.answer: Je reste jusqu’à ce que le guichet ferme. Après que le guichet a fermé, je suis rentré.

takeaways: The trigger, not the meaning of the verb, calls the subjunctive.
Stem from `ils` minus `-ent`; six irregular verbs to memorise.
Same subject equals infinitive; `après que` keeps the indicative.

lessons.title: Les constructions infinitives de temps et de but
lessons.summary: Use `avant de` plus infinitive for an action that comes first, and `après` plus past infinitive (`avoir` or `être` plus participle) for an action already completed. With a reflexive verb the past infinitive is `après s’être` plus participle. For purpose, use `pour` or `afin de` plus infinitive when both verbs share a subject, and `pour que` or `afin que` plus subjunctive when they do not.
objectives: Build a past infinitive with the correct auxiliary.
Choose between an infinitive and a subjunctive clause for purpose.
Avoid the bare `après` plus infinitive pattern.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: An infinitive names an action without marking a subject or a tense, which is why French uses it whenever the subject is already clear. `Avant de` is always followed by a simple infinitive: `Avant de signer le bail, elle a vérifié les conditions`. `Après` requires the past infinitive, because the action is already finished: `Après avoir rempli le formulaire, je l’ai envoyé`. Choose the auxiliary exactly as in the compound past, so movement and reflexive verbs use `être`: `après être arrivée`, `après s’être installée`.

Purpose works on the subject test. One subject allows an infinitive: `Je suis cette formation pour améliorer mon français`. Two subjects require a conjunction plus the subjunctive: `Je vous écris afin que vous compreniez ma situation`. Writing `après` directly in front of a simple infinitive is not standard; in careful French it must be the past infinitive.
points: Use `avant de` plus a simple infinitive for the earlier action.
Use `après` plus `avoir` or `être` plus participle for a completed action.
Choose the past-infinitive auxiliary with the compound-past rules.
Use `après s’être` plus participle with a reflexive verb, agreeing where required.
Switch to `pour que` or `afin que` plus subjunctive as soon as the subject changes.

examples.french: Après avoir rempli le formulaire, je l’ai envoyé au ministère.
examples.english: After completing the form, I sent it to the ministry.
examples.note: Past infinitive with avoir.

examples.french: Après s’être installée à Montréal, elle a cherché un emploi bilingue.
examples.english: After settling in Montreal, she looked for a bilingual job.
examples.note: Reflexive past infinitive; the participle agrees with the subject.

examples.french: Avant de signer le bail, elle a vérifié toutes les conditions.
examples.english: Before signing the lease, she checked all the conditions.
examples.note: « Avant de » takes a simple infinitive.

examples.french: Je suis cette formation pour améliorer mon français professionnel.
examples.english: I am taking this course to improve my professional French.
examples.note: One subject, so an infinitive is enough.

examples.french: La ville a modifié l’horaire afin que les familles puissent participer.
examples.english: The city changed the schedule so that families could take part.
examples.note: Two subjects, so a conjunction plus the subjunctive.

mistakes.avoid: Après courir, je me repose quelques minutes.
mistakes.prefer: Après avoir couru, je me repose quelques minutes.
mistakes.why: `Après` requires the past infinitive when the action is already completed.

mistakes.avoid: J’ai écrit une lettre pour que je clarifie ma situation.
mistakes.prefer: J’ai écrit une lettre pour clarifier ma situation.
mistakes.why: With a single subject French uses `pour` plus infinitive, not `pour que`.

vocabulary.example: Après s’être installés, ils ont inscrit les enfants à l’école du quartier.
vocabulary.note: Reflexive verb; the past infinitive is `après s’être installé(e)(s)`.

vocabulary.example: Avant de signer, vérifiez la durée du bail et le montant du loyer.
vocabulary.note: Regular `-er` verb; frequent in administrative instructions.

vocabulary.example: Un bail signé engage le locataire pour douze mois.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; irregular plural `des baux`.

vocabulary.example: Un ministère provincial gère les demandes de reconnaissance de diplôme.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; not to be confused with `une ministre`, the person.

practice.prompt: Rewrite with a past infinitive: « Elle est arrivée, puis elle a téléphoné au bureau. »
practice.hint: `Arriver` takes `être`, so the participle agrees.
practice.answer: Après être arrivée, elle a téléphoné au bureau.

takeaways: `Avant de` plus infinitive, `après` plus past infinitive.
The past infinitive follows the compound-past auxiliary rules.
One subject equals `pour`; two subjects equal `pour que` plus subjunctive.
keywords: infinitive constructions for sequence and purpose

lessons.title: Le participe présent et le gérondif
lessons.summary: Form the present participle from the present `nous` form minus `-ons` plus `-ant`: `nous travaillons` gives `travaillant`. Three verbs are irregular: `ayant`, `étant`, `sachant`. Adding `en` gives the gerund, which expresses simultaneity, manner, or means and requires the same understood subject as the main verb. The present participle without `en` can instead express cause or a relative-like description.
objectives: Form the present participle, including the three irregular verbs.
Use `en` plus participle for simultaneity, manner, or means.
Keep the subject of the gerund identical to the subject of the main verb.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: The present participle is the `-ant` form. It is built on the present `nous` stem, so it inherits any spelling change from that form: `nous commençons` gives `commençant`, `nous mangeons` gives `mangeant`. Only `avoir`, `être`, and `savoir` are irregular, giving `ayant`, `étant`, and `sachant`.

Adding `en` produces the gerund, which places two actions of the same subject side by side. It can express simultaneity (`En travaillant, elle a appris beaucoup de vocabulaire`), manner or means (`Elle a trouvé un logement en consultant les annonces`). The constraint is strict: the subject of the gerund must be the subject of the main verb, so a sentence like `En arrivant, le dossier était prêt` is faulty because a file cannot arrive. Without `en`, the participle instead gives a cause or a description: `Ayant acquis une solide expérience, elle a dirigé le projet`.
points: Take the present `nous` form and replace `-ons` with `-ant`.
Keep the spelling change of the `nous` form: `commençant`, `mangeant`.
Memorise `ayant`, `étant`, `sachant`.
Add `en` for simultaneity, manner, or means.
Check that the gerund and the main verb share the same subject.

examples.french: En travaillant avec une équipe bilingue, elle a enrichi son vocabulaire.
examples.english: By working with a bilingual team, she expanded her vocabulary.
examples.note: Gerund of means, same subject as the main verb.

examples.french: Elle a trouvé un logement en consultant les annonces du quartier.
examples.english: She found housing by looking through the local listings.
examples.note: Gerund of manner.

examples.french: En arrivant au bureau, j’ai remarqué que la file était déjà longue.
examples.english: On arriving at the office, I noticed that the queue was already long.
examples.note: Simultaneity; the subject of both verbs is « je ».

examples.french: Ayant acquis une solide expérience, elle a dirigé le projet avec assurance.
examples.english: Having gained solid experience, she led the project confidently.
examples.note: Participle without « en »: cause rather than simultaneity.

examples.french: Ne sachant pas où déposer le dossier, il a téléphoné à la mairie.
examples.english: Not knowing where to submit the file, he phoned the town hall.
examples.note: Irregular participle « sachant » in a causal construction.

mistakes.avoid: En arrivant au guichet, le dossier était déjà complet.
mistakes.prefer: En arrivant au guichet, j’avais déjà un dossier complet.
mistakes.why: The gerund must share the subject of the main verb, and a file cannot arrive.

mistakes.avoid: En sachant la réponse, elle a levé la main.
mistakes.prefer: Sachant la réponse, elle a levé la main.
mistakes.why: `Savoir` expresses a state, so the causal participle without `en` is the natural form.

vocabulary.example: Ayant acquis de l’expérience à l’étranger, elle a été retenue immédiatement.
vocabulary.note: Irregular verb; participle `acquis`, present participle `acquérant`.

vocabulary.example: En consultant le site du ministère, j’ai trouvé la liste des documents.
vocabulary.note: Regular `-er` verb; very useful with the gerund of means.

vocabulary.example: Un stage en milieu bilingue complète utilement une formation.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; `un stagiaire` is the intern.

vocabulary.example: Une équipe bilingue répond aux appels du lundi au vendredi.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; takes a singular verb in French.

practice.prompt: Join with a gerund: « Elle prépare son entrevue. Elle relit les annonces. »
practice.hint: Both actions belong to the same subject.
practice.answer: Elle prépare son entrevue en relisant les annonces.

takeaways: `Nous` form minus `-ons` plus `-ant`, with three irregular verbs.
`En` plus participle equals simultaneity, manner, or means.
Different subjects make the gerund ungrammatical.
keywords: the present participle and en + participle

lessons.title: La voix passive et les tournures pronominales
lessons.summary: The passive is `être` plus past participle, and the participle agrees with the subject: `les demandes ont été traitées`. The agent, when named, is introduced by `par`. French often prefers two alternatives: a pronominal construction with `se` for a general process (`Cette démarche se fait en ligne`), and `on` plus an active verb for an unspecified human agent (`On m’a informé`).
objectives: Build a passive sentence with the correct agreement.
Replace a heavy passive with a pronominal construction where it is idiomatic.
Use `on` for an unnamed human agent.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: In a passive sentence the grammatical subject receives the action instead of performing it. French forms it with `être` in the required tense plus the past participle, which agrees with that subject: `Le formulaire a été envoyé`, `Les demandes ont été traitées`. If the agent is mentioned, `par` introduces it: `Le rapport a été rédigé par le comité`.

French uses the passive less than English and has two natural alternatives. A pronominal construction with `se` describes a general process or property, with no agent in view: `Cette démarche se fait entièrement en ligne`, `Ce produit se vend bien`. The pronoun `on` plus an active verb covers an unspecified but human agent and is the usual spoken equivalent of an English passive: `On m’a indiqué que le service fermerait plus tôt`.
points: Conjugate `être` in the tense you need, then add the participle.
Agree the participle with the subject, not with the agent.
Introduce a named agent with `par`.
Use `se` plus verb for a general process with no agent.
Use `on` plus an active verb when the agent is human but unnamed.

examples.french: Le formulaire a été envoyé par voie électronique.
examples.english: The form was sent electronically.
examples.note: Passive with a masculine singular subject.

examples.french: Les demandes ont été traitées en priorité cette semaine.
examples.english: The applications were processed as a priority this week.
examples.note: The participle agrees with the feminine plural subject.

examples.french: Le rapport a été rédigé par le comité de quartier.
examples.english: The report was written by the neighbourhood committee.
examples.note: The agent is introduced by « par ».

examples.french: Cette démarche se fait entièrement en ligne.
examples.english: This procedure is completed entirely online.
examples.note: Pronominal construction for a general process.

examples.french: On m’a indiqué que le service fermerait plus tôt aujourd’hui.
examples.english: I was told that the service would close earlier today.
examples.note: « On » replaces an English passive with an unnamed agent.

mistakes.avoid: Les demandes ont été traité la semaine dernière.
mistakes.prefer: Les demandes ont été traitées la semaine dernière.
mistakes.why: In the passive the participle agrees with the subject, here feminine plural.

mistakes.avoid: Le formulaire a été envoyer par voie électronique.
mistakes.prefer: Le formulaire a été envoyé par voie électronique.
mistakes.why: The passive is built with a past participle, `envoyé`, not with the infinitive `envoyer`, which sounds identical.

vocabulary.example: Les dossiers sont traités dans l’ordre d’arrivée.
vocabulary.note: Regular `-er` verb; `le traitement` is the related noun.

vocabulary.english: to be done, to take place
vocabulary.example: L’inscription se fait en ligne jusqu’au 30 juin.
vocabulary.note: Pronominal construction used instead of a passive with no agent.

vocabulary.example: Un avis officiel a été publié sur le site de la municipalité.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; identical in the plural.

vocabulary.example: Un comité consultatif examine les projets de rénovation.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; the ending -té is usually feminine, so this one must be learned.

practice.prompt: Rewrite without a passive: « Les décisions sont prises par une commission. » and « The forms are filled in online. »
practice.hint: One keeps a named agent, the other has none.
practice.answer: Une commission prend les décisions. Les formulaires se remplissent en ligne.

takeaways: `Être` plus participle, agreeing with the subject; agent after `par`.
`Se` plus verb for a process with no agent.
`On` plus active verb is the everyday equivalent of an English passive.

lessons.title: Le passé récent
lessons.summary: The recent past is the fixed pattern `venir de` plus infinitive: it states that an action has just happened. Only `venir` is conjugated, and `de` is obligatory. In the present it means has just; in the imperfect (`je venais de`) it means had just. Do not confuse it with `venir` plus infinitive without `de`, which expresses movement in order to do something.
objectives: Conjugate `venir` correctly for each subject.
Keep `de` before the infinitive in every person.
Distinguish the recent past from `venir` used as a movement verb.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: The recent past is a periphrasis: a fixed group of words replacing a single tense. `Venir` carries the person and the tense, `de` links the two verbs, and the second verb stays in the infinitive: `Je viens de terminer`, `Nous venons de recevoir`, `Le ministère vient d’annoncer`. `De` elides to `d’` before a vowel.

Two contrasts matter. First, tense: `je viens de déposer` means I have just submitted, while `je venais de déposer` means I had just submitted and situates the action before another past moment. Second, structure: without `de`, `venir` plus infinitive keeps its movement meaning, so `Je viens terminer la réunion` means I am coming in order to finish the meeting, which is not the recent past at all.
points: Conjugate `venir` for the subject: `je viens`, `nous venons`, `ils viennent`.
Insert `de` or `d’` before the infinitive, without exception.
Leave the second verb in the infinitive, never in a participle.
Use the imperfect `venais de` for had just.
Read `venir` plus bare infinitive as movement, not as recent past.

examples.french: Je viens de terminer mon entrevue d’embauche.
examples.english: I have just finished my job interview.
examples.note: Present of venir plus de plus infinitive.

examples.french: Le ministère vient d’annoncer une nouvelle mesure de soutien.
examples.english: The ministry has just announced a new support measure.
examples.note: « De » elides before a vowel.

examples.french: Nous venons de recevoir votre demande de logement.
examples.english: We have just received your housing application.
examples.note: Only venir changes for the subject.

examples.french: Je venais de déposer le dossier quand le guichet a fermé.
examples.english: I had just submitted the file when the counter closed.
examples.note: Imperfect of venir for an action just completed in the past.

examples.french: Je viens terminer la réunion avec vous, puis je repars.
examples.english: I am coming to finish the meeting with you, then I am leaving again.
examples.note: Without « de », venir keeps its movement meaning.

mistakes.avoid: Je viens terminer la réunion il y a deux minutes.
mistakes.prefer: Je viens de terminer la réunion il y a deux minutes.
mistakes.why: Without `de`, the sentence expresses movement, not a just-completed action.

mistakes.avoid: Nous venons de reçu votre demande.
mistakes.prefer: Nous venons de recevoir votre demande.
mistakes.why: The recent past takes an infinitive, never a past participle.

vocabulary.example: Elle vient de recevoir sa confirmation d’inscription.
vocabulary.note: Fixed pattern; only `venir` is conjugated and `de` is obligatory.

vocabulary.example: La ville vient d’annoncer la gratuité des transports le dimanche.
vocabulary.note: `-cer` verb: cedilla before `a` and `o`.

vocabulary.example: Une réunion d’information vient de se terminer dans la grande salle.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; `se réunir` is the related verb.

vocabulary.example: Une mesure de soutien temporaire aide les familles à faible revenu.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun phrase; the gender comes from `mesure`.

practice.prompt: Say in French that the service has just closed, and that it had just closed when you arrived.
practice.hint: Present of `venir` first, then the imperfect.
practice.answer: Le service vient de fermer. Le service venait de fermer quand je suis arrivé.

takeaways: `Venir de` plus infinitive equals has just.
`Venais de` plus infinitive equals had just.
Dropping `de` turns the sentence back into movement.

modules.title: Les pronoms, les questions et la négation
modules.description: Track references, place pronouns correctly, ask questions, and form natural negation.

lessons.title: Les pronoms compléments directs et indirects
lessons.summary: A direct object follows the verb with no preposition and is replaced by `me, te, le, la, nous, vous, les`. A person introduced by `à` is replaced by `me, te, lui, nous, vous, leur`. The pronoun goes before the conjugated verb or auxiliary, and before the infinitive it belongs to. When two pronouns meet, the order is fixed: `me/te/nous/vous` before `le/la/les`, and `le/la/les` before `lui/leur`.
objectives: Test a verb’s construction before choosing a pronoun.
Position a single pronoun correctly in simple, compound, and infinitive structures.
Apply the fixed order when two pronouns appear together.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: The pronoun is decided by the French verb, not by the English translation. `Voir quelqu’un` and `regarder quelque chose` take a direct object, so they use `le`, `la`, `les`. `Parler à quelqu’un`, `téléphoner à quelqu’un`, `répondre à quelqu’un`, and `envoyer quelque chose à quelqu’un` take an indirect object, so they use `lui` and `leur`. Several verbs that are direct in English are indirect in French, and that mismatch is the main source of error.

Placement follows the verb group. Before a single conjugated verb: `Elle nous reçoit`. Before the auxiliary in a compound tense: `Elle nous a reçus`. Before the infinitive when the pronoun belongs to it: `Je dois le remplir`. When two pronouns occur, French uses one fixed order: `me`, `te`, `nous`, `vous` come first; then `le`, `la`, `les`; then `lui`, `leur`; then `y`; then `en`. So you say `Je les lui remettrai` and `Elle me les a envoyés`.
points: Check whether the French verb takes a direct object or `à` plus a person.
Use `le`, `la`, `les` for a direct object and `lui`, `leur` for a person after `à`.
Place the pronoun before the conjugated verb, or before the auxiliary in a compound tense.
Attach the pronoun to the infinitive it completes: `Je vais le remplir`.
Follow the fixed sequence `me/te/nous/vous`, then `le/la/les`, then `lui/leur`.

examples.french: La conseillère nous reçoit à neuf heures.
examples.english: The adviser is meeting us at nine o’clock.
examples.note: « Recevoir quelqu’un » is direct.

examples.french: Je leur envoie les documents demandés dès ce soir.
examples.english: I am sending them the requested documents this evening.
examples.note: « Envoyer à quelqu’un » is indirect, so « leur ».

examples.french: Ce formulaire est long, mais je dois le remplir avant vendredi.
examples.english: This form is long, but I have to complete it before Friday.
examples.note: The pronoun goes before the infinitive it belongs to.

examples.french: Les documents ? Je les lui remettrai demain matin.
examples.english: The documents? I will hand them to him tomorrow morning.
examples.note: Direct pronoun before indirect pronoun.

examples.french: Elle m’a téléphoné hier pour confirmer le rendez-vous.
examples.english: She phoned me yesterday to confirm the appointment.
examples.note: « Téléphoner à quelqu’un » is indirect in French, unlike its English equivalent.

mistakes.avoid: Je l’ai téléphoné pour confirmer.
mistakes.prefer: Je lui ai téléphoné pour confirmer.
mistakes.why: `Téléphoner à quelqu’un` takes an indirect object, so the pronoun is `lui`.

mistakes.avoid: Je vais remplir le demain.
mistakes.prefer: Je vais le remplir demain.
mistakes.why: The pronoun stands before the infinitive it completes, not after it.

vocabulary.example: J’ai téléphoné à la conseillère, puis je lui ai envoyé un courriel.
vocabulary.note: Indirect in French even though the English verb is direct.

vocabulary.example: Je les lui remettrai avant la fin de la semaine.
vocabulary.note: Follows `mettre`; participle `remis`.

vocabulary.example: Un document numérisé est accepté pour la première étape.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; `un justificatif` is the narrower administrative term.

vocabulary.example: Un rendez-vous en personne reste nécessaire pour la signature.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; invariable in the plural.

practice.prompt: Replace the underlined groups: « J’envoie le dossier à la conseillère. »
practice.hint: Direct pronoun first, then indirect.
practice.answer: Je le lui envoie.

takeaways: The French verb decides: direct object or `à` plus person.
`Lui` and `leur` are for people introduced by `à`.
Fixed order: `me/te/nous/vous`, `le/la/les`, `lui/leur`, `y`, `en`.

lessons.title: Les pronoms « y » et « en »
lessons.summary: `Y` replaces a place or a non-person complement introduced by `à`: `Je vais au bureau` gives `J’y vais`; `Je pense au projet` gives `J’y pense`. `En` replaces a complement introduced by `de`, a partitive phrase, or a counted noun: `Je parle du projet` gives `J’en parle`; `J’ai deux dossiers` gives `J’en ai deux`. For a person, keep a stressed pronoun: `Je pense à elle`, `Je parle d’elle`.
objectives: Find the preposition of the phrase you want to replace.
Keep the quantity expression when using `en`.
Use a stressed pronoun instead of `y` or `en` for people.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: `Y` and `en` are adverbial pronouns: they stand for a whole prepositional phrase rather than for a noun alone. The preposition of the original phrase decides which one you need. Anything built with `à` and referring to a thing or a place becomes `y`; anything built with `de` and referring to a thing becomes `en`. `En` also covers the partitive (`du café` gives `j’en bois`) and any counted noun (`deux formations` gives `j’en ai suivi deux`).

Two details complete the rule. First, a quantity word stays in the sentence after `en`: `J’en veux deux`, `Il y en a beaucoup`. Second, people are excluded: with `penser à`, `s’intéresser à`, `parler de` about a person, French keeps a stressed pronoun, so `Je pense à elle` and not `J’y pense`. Placement is the same as for object pronouns: before the conjugated verb or auxiliary, and before the infinitive they belong to.
points: Identify the preposition before choosing between `y` and `en`.
Use `y` for `à` plus a thing or a place, `en` for `de` plus a thing.
Use `en` for a partitive article and for any counted noun.
Repeat the number or quantity after `en`.
Keep `à elle`, `de lui`, and other stressed forms for people.

examples.french: Vous allez au centre de services ? Oui, j’y vais cet après-midi.
examples.english: Are you going to the service centre? Yes, I am going there this afternoon.
examples.note: « Y » replaces « au centre de services ».

examples.french: Avez-vous besoin de renseignements ? Oui, j’en ai besoin.
examples.english: Do you need information? Yes, I need some.
examples.note: « Avoir besoin de » becomes « en ».

examples.french: Elle a suivi deux formations cette année ; elle en a suivi deux.
examples.english: She took two training courses this year; she took two of them.
examples.note: The number stays after « en ».

examples.french: Ce projet est important : nous y pensons depuis des mois.
examples.english: This project is important: we have been thinking about it for months.
examples.note: « Penser à » plus a thing gives « y ».

examples.french: Ma conseillère est excellente ; je pense souvent à elle.
examples.english: My adviser is excellent; I often think about her.
examples.note: With a person, a stressed pronoun replaces « y ».

mistakes.avoid: J’en vais à l’école chaque matin.
mistakes.prefer: J’y vais chaque matin.
mistakes.why: A place introduced by `à` is replaced by `y`, not by `en`.

mistakes.avoid: Ma sœur habite ici ; j’y pense souvent.
mistakes.prefer: Ma sœur habite ici ; je pense souvent à elle.
mistakes.why: `Y` does not replace a person; French uses a stressed pronoun.

vocabulary.example: Nous parlons du projet en réunion, et nous en parlons aussi entre nous.
vocabulary.note: Built with `de`, so the complement is replaced by `en`.

vocabulary.example: Je pense à ma prochaine entrevue, et j’y pense chaque soir.
vocabulary.note: `Y` for a thing, but `à lui` or `à elle` for a person.

vocabulary.example: Un renseignement précis évite un déplacement inutile.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun, frequently used in the plural: `des renseignements`.

vocabulary.example: Un centre de services regroupe plusieurs démarches administratives.
vocabulary.note: Masculine compound noun; learn it as one unit.

practice.prompt: Answer with `y` or `en`: « Combien de dossiers avez-vous déposés ? » (three) and « Allez-vous à la mairie ? » (yes).
practice.hint: One answer keeps a number.
practice.answer: J’en ai déposé trois. Oui, j’y vais.

takeaways: `À` plus thing gives `y`; `de` plus thing gives `en`.
`En` also covers partitives and counted nouns, and the number stays.
People keep stressed pronouns: `à elle`, `de lui`.

lessons.title: Les pronoms toniques, réfléchis et emphatiques
lessons.summary: Stressed pronouns (`moi, toi, lui, elle, nous, vous, eux, elles`) are used after a preposition, in a coordinated subject, after `c’est`, and for emphasis. In a coordinated subject, politeness puts the first person last: `Elle et moi`, `Marie et moi`. Reflexive pronouns (`me, te, se, nous, vous, se`) belong to the verb and refer back to its subject. `Soi` is the stressed form used with an indefinite subject such as `on` or `chacun`.
objectives: Use a stressed pronoun in each of its four contexts.
Order a coordinated subject according to French convention.
Choose `soi` and `soi-même` with an indefinite subject.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: A stressed pronoun stands on its own, away from the verb. French requires it in four situations: after any preposition (`avec lui`, `chez elle`, `pour eux`), in a coordinated subject (`Elle et moi participerons`), after `c’est` (`C’est moi`), and for contrast or emphasis (`Moi, je préfère attendre`). Adding `-même` reinforces it: `moi-même`, `eux-mêmes`.

In a coordinated subject, French convention names the first person last, so `Elle et moi` and `Marie et moi`, not the reverse. Reflexive pronouns work differently: they are part of the verb and point back at the subject, as in `elle se prépare`, `nous nous inscrivons`. When the subject is indefinite — `on`, `chacun`, `tout le monde`, or an infinitive used generally — the stressed form is `soi`: `Il vaut mieux vérifier le formulaire soi-même`.
points: Use a stressed pronoun immediately after any preposition.
Place the first person last in a coordinated subject: `Elle et moi`.
Use `c’est moi`, `c’est lui`, `ce sont eux` to identify.
Add `-même` for emphasis, agreeing in number: `nous-mêmes`, `eux-mêmes`.
Use `soi` and `soi-même` when the subject is `on`, `chacun`, or unspecified.

examples.french: Elle et moi participerons à la consultation publique de jeudi.
examples.english: She and I will take part in Thursday’s public consultation.
examples.note: The first person comes last in a coordinated subject.

examples.french: Le rendez-vous a lieu chez elle, pas au bureau.
examples.english: The appointment is at her place, not at the office.
examples.note: Stressed pronoun after a preposition.

examples.french: Ils ont préparé le dossier eux-mêmes, sans aide extérieure.
examples.english: They prepared the file themselves, without outside help.
examples.note: Emphatic form agreeing in number.

examples.french: Il vaut mieux vérifier le formulaire soi-même avant de l’envoyer.
examples.english: It is better to check the form oneself before sending it.
examples.note: « Soi » with an impersonal subject.

examples.french: Moi, je préfère déposer le dossier en personne.
examples.english: Personally, I prefer to submit the file in person.
examples.note: Stressed pronoun in front for contrast.

mistakes.avoid: Moi et ma collègue avons rédigé le rapport.
mistakes.prefer: Ma collègue et moi avons rédigé le rapport.
mistakes.why: French convention places the first-person pronoun last in a coordinated subject.

mistakes.avoid: Chacun doit préparer son dossier lui-même ou elle-même selon le cas.
mistakes.prefer: Chacun doit préparer son dossier soi-même.
mistakes.why: With the indefinite subject `chacun`, the stressed form is `soi`.

vocabulary.example: Une consultation publique permet à chacun de s’exprimer sur le projet.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun phrase; the gender comes from `consultation`.

vocabulary.example: Elle se prépare seule pour l’entrevue de mardi.
vocabulary.note: Reflexive verb; the pronoun changes with the subject.

vocabulary.example: Il vaut mieux relire son dossier soi-même avant de l’envoyer.
vocabulary.note: Used with `on`, `chacun`, or an impersonal construction.

vocabulary.example: Ma collègue et moi partageons le même bureau.
vocabulary.note: Feminine form; the masculine is `un collègue`, with the same spelling.

practice.prompt: Rewrite politely: « Moi et lui avons déposé la demande. »
practice.hint: Two changes: order, and the stressed form for the third person.
practice.answer: Lui et moi avons déposé la demande.

takeaways: Preposition, coordination, `c’est`, emphasis: four homes for stressed pronouns.
Name yourself last: `Elle et moi`.
Indefinite subject equals `soi` and `soi-même`.

lessons.title: Les indéfinis « tout », « quelqu’un », « chacun », « n’importe » et « autre »
lessons.summary: `Tout` agrees when it determines a noun (`tout le dossier`, `toutes les candidates`) but is invariable as an adverb (`tout simplement`). `Quelqu’un` and `quelque chose` take `de` before an adjective: `quelqu’un d’autre`, `quelque chose d’important`. `Chacun` and `chacune` are singular and take `de` or `d’entre`. `N’importe qui`, `n’importe quoi`, and `n’importe quel` express free choice in positive sentences; the negative counterparts are `personne` and `rien`. `Autre` varies with specificity: `un autre`, `l’autre`, `les autres`, `d’autres`.
objectives: Agree `tout` correctly and recognise its invariable adverbial use.
Insert `de` before an adjective after `quelqu’un` and `quelque chose`.
Select the right form of `autre` and of the `n’importe` series.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: An indefinite word refers without identifying a precise person or thing. `Tout` has four determiner forms — `tout`, `toute`, `tous`, `toutes` — and is normally followed by another determiner: `tout le dossier`, `toutes les candidates`. As a pronoun it means everything (`Tout est prêt`), and before an adjective or adverb it becomes an invariable intensifier: `tout simplement`, `tout près`.

`Quelqu’un` and `quelque chose` are singular and insert `de` before any adjective: `quelqu’un de disponible`, `quelque chose d’utile`, `quelqu’un d’autre`. `Chacun` and `chacune` are always singular and take `de` or `d’entre` before a group: `chacune des candidates`, `chacun d’entre vous`. The `n’importe` series expresses free choice and is used in positive sentences only: `n’importe qui`, `n’importe quoi`, `n’importe quel formulaire`; the negatives are `personne` and `rien`. Finally, `autre` is graded by specificity: `un autre` (another one), `l’autre` (the other specific one), `les autres` (the others), `d’autres` (some others).
points: Agree `tout` with the noun group it introduces, and leave it invariable before an adjective.
Add `de` between `quelqu’un` or `quelque chose` and any adjective.
Keep `chacun` and `chacune` singular, followed by `de` or `d’entre`.
Use the `n’importe` series only in positive sentences.
Choose among `un autre`, `l’autre`, `les autres`, and `d’autres` by specificity.

examples.french: Toutes les candidates ont reçu les mêmes consignes écrites.
examples.english: All the candidates received the same written instructions.
examples.note: « Tout » agrees with the noun group it introduces.

examples.french: Quelqu’un d’autre pourra-t-il m’expliquer cette démarche ?
examples.english: Will someone else be able to explain this procedure to me?
examples.note: « De » is required before the adjective.

examples.french: Chacun d’entre vous peut proposer une solution concrète.
examples.english: Each of you can suggest a concrete solution.
examples.note: « Chacun » stays singular and takes « d’entre ».

examples.french: Prenez n’importe quel formulaire vert ; les autres sont périmés.
examples.english: Take any green form at all; the others are out of date.
examples.note: Free choice in a positive sentence, then « les autres » for a known group.

examples.french: Personne n’a répondu et rien n’a été décidé pendant la réunion.
examples.english: Nobody answered and nothing was decided during the meeting.
examples.note: Negative counterparts of the n’importe series.

mistakes.avoid: Je cherche quelqu’un disponible cet après-midi.
mistakes.prefer: Je cherche quelqu’un de disponible cet après-midi.
mistakes.why: `Quelqu’un` requires `de` before an adjective.

mistakes.avoid: Chacune des candidates ont reçu une réponse.
mistakes.prefer: Chacune des candidates a reçu une réponse.
mistakes.why: `Chacune` is singular, so the verb stays in the singular.

vocabulary.example: Une consigne claire évite beaucoup d’erreurs pendant l’épreuve.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; `suivre les consignes` means to follow instructions.

vocabulary.example: Une candidate motivée pose des questions précises en entrevue.
vocabulary.note: Feminine form; the masculine is `un candidat`.

vocabulary.example: N’importe quelle pièce d’identité officielle est acceptée.
vocabulary.note: Determiner form; it agrees with the noun that follows.

vocabulary.example: Chacun d’entre nous doit relire son dossier avant l’envoi.
vocabulary.note: Always singular, even when the group is plural.

practice.prompt: Complete: « ___ les documents sont prêts, mais il manque ___ d’important : ___ des candidats doit signer. »
practice.hint: Agreement, then `de` before an adjective, then a singular indefinite.
practice.answer: Tous les documents sont prêts, mais il manque quelque chose d’important : chacun des candidats doit signer.

takeaways: `Tout` agrees as a determiner and is invariable as an intensifier.
`Quelqu’un` and `quelque chose` need `de` before an adjective.
`N’importe` for free choice, `personne` and `rien` for negation.
keywords: tout, quelqu’un, chacun, n’importe, and autre

lessons.title: La négation et la place des pronoms
lessons.summary: In careful French, `ne` precedes the verb group and the second element (`pas`, `jamais`, `plus`, `rien`, `personne`, `que`) follows the conjugated verb or the auxiliary. Object and reflexive pronouns sit between `ne` and the verb. With an infinitive, both negative words come together in front: `ne pas répondre`. `Ne` is often dropped in speech but must be kept in formal writing, and `si` replaces `oui` when contradicting a negative.
objectives: Position both negative elements in simple and compound tenses.
Keep pronouns inside the negation.
Contradict a negative statement with `si`.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: French negation has two parts. `Ne` attaches to the left of the verb group, and the second word follows the conjugated verb: `Le portail ne fonctionne plus`. In a compound tense the second word comes after the auxiliary, not after the participle: `Je ne l’ai jamais reçu`. Object and reflexive pronouns belong inside the frame, right after `ne`: `Je ne le connais pas`, `Il ne s’est pas inscrit`.

Two structures behave differently. Before an infinitive, both negative words stay together: `Je préfère ne pas répondre aujourd’hui`. And `personne` as an object comes after the participle: `Je n’ai vu personne`. Register matters: dropping `ne` is normal in speech but unacceptable in an exam text or a formal letter. Finally, French distinguishes two ways of saying yes: `oui` answers a positive question, while `si` contradicts a negative question or statement.
points: Write `ne` before the pronouns and the conjugated verb.
Place `pas`, `jamais`, or `plus` after the conjugated verb or the auxiliary.
Keep `ne pas` together in front of an infinitive.
Place `personne` after the past participle when it is the object.
Answer a negative question with `si`, never with `oui`.

examples.french: Le portail ne fonctionne plus depuis hier soir.
examples.english: The portal has not been working since yesterday evening.
examples.note: Simple tense: « ne » before the verb, « plus » after it.

examples.french: Je ne l’ai jamais reçu malgré mes deux demandes.
examples.english: I never received it despite my two requests.
examples.note: Compound tense: the second element follows the auxiliary.

examples.french: Il ne s’est pas inscrit avant la date limite.
examples.english: He did not register before the deadline.
examples.note: The reflexive pronoun stays inside the negation.

examples.french: Je préfère ne pas répondre avant d’avoir vérifié les faits.
examples.english: I prefer not to answer before checking the facts.
examples.note: Both negative words stand together before an infinitive.

examples.french: Vous n’avez pas encore soumis le formulaire ? Si, je l’ai soumis ce matin.
examples.english: Have you not submitted the form yet? Yes, I submitted it this morning.
examples.note: « Si » contradicts a negative question.

mistakes.avoid: Je le connais pas et je l’ai vu jamais.
mistakes.prefer: Je ne le connais pas et je ne l’ai jamais vu.
mistakes.why: `Ne` must be kept in careful French, and the second element follows the auxiliary.

mistakes.avoid: Il a ne pas répondu à ma demande.
mistakes.prefer: Il n’a pas répondu à ma demande.
mistakes.why: In a compound tense, `ne` precedes the auxiliary and `pas` follows it.

vocabulary.example: Je ne connais pas encore la décision du comité.
vocabulary.note: Basic frame; `ne` precedes the verb group, `pas` follows the conjugated verb.

vocabulary.example: Elle n’a jamais manqué une séance de formation.
vocabulary.note: Rules out every occurrence; same placement as `ne… pas`.

vocabulary.example: Le guichet n’accepte plus les paiements en espèces.
vocabulary.note: Marks a situation that has stopped.

vocabulary.example: Un portail sécurisé permet de suivre l’état de sa demande.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; also means a gate.

practice.prompt: Make negative, keeping the pronoun: « Je lui ai envoyé le formulaire. » (never)
practice.hint: The pronoun stays between `ne` and the auxiliary.
practice.answer: Je ne lui ai jamais envoyé le formulaire.

takeaways: `Ne` hugs the verb group; the second word follows the conjugated verb.
Pronouns live inside the negation, `ne pas` lives in front of an infinitive.
`Si` is the yes that contradicts a negative.

lessons.title: L’accord avec une phrase affirmative ou négative
lessons.summary: To echo someone, match the polarity of their statement. After a positive statement use `moi aussi`, `lui aussi`, `nous aussi`. After a negative statement use `moi non plus`, `elle non plus`. `Non plus` also adds a second excluded element: `Elle n’utilise pas la voiture, et son conjoint non plus`. Using `aussi` after a negative is one of the most audible learner errors.
objectives: Identify whether the first statement is positive or negative.
Respond with the matching stressed pronoun and particle.
Add a second excluded element with `non plus`.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: Polarity is simply whether a sentence affirms or denies. French marks agreement with a previous speaker by copying that polarity: a positive statement is echoed with `aussi`, a negative statement with `non plus`. The person is expressed by a stressed pronoun placed first: `moi aussi`, `toi non plus`, `eux aussi`.

The same particle works inside a single sentence when you add a second element to what has already been said. After a positive clause: `Elle participe à l’atelier, et son conjoint aussi`. After a negative clause: `Elle n’utilise pas la voiture, et son conjoint non plus`. English uses too and either, and English speakers regularly transfer too into a negative context, which produces the incorrect `moi aussi` after a denial.
points: Read the first statement and label it positive or negative.
Echo a positive statement with `aussi`.
Echo a negative statement with `non plus`.
Start with the stressed pronoun: `moi`, `toi`, `lui`, `elle`, `nous`, `vous`, `eux`, `elles`.
Use `non plus` to add a second excluded element after a negative clause.

examples.french: Je participe à l’atelier du samedi. — Moi aussi !
examples.english: I go to the Saturday workshop. — So do I!
examples.note: Positive statement echoed with « aussi ».

examples.french: Je ne peux pas travailler dimanche. — Moi non plus !
examples.english: I cannot work on Sunday. — Neither can I!
examples.note: Negative statement echoed with « non plus ».

examples.french: Elle n’utilise pas la voiture, et son conjoint non plus.
examples.english: She does not use the car, and neither does her partner.
examples.note: A second excluded element inside the same sentence.

examples.french: Il a déposé sa demande en ligne, et sa sœur aussi.
examples.english: He submitted his application online, and so did his sister.
examples.note: A second included element after a positive clause.

examples.french: Nous n’avons pas reçu la confirmation. — Nous non plus.
examples.english: We have not received the confirmation. — Neither have we.
examples.note: The stressed pronoun comes first.

mistakes.avoid: Je n’ai pas compris la consigne. — Moi aussi.
mistakes.prefer: Je n’ai pas compris la consigne. — Moi non plus.
mistakes.why: A negative statement is echoed with `non plus`, never with `aussi`.

mistakes.avoid: Elle n’aime pas les longues réunions, et son collègue aussi.
mistakes.prefer: Elle n’aime pas les longues réunions, et son collègue non plus.
mistakes.why: The added element is also excluded, so it takes `non plus`.

vocabulary.example: Je ne travaille pas le dimanche. — Moi non plus.
vocabulary.note: Reply used only after a negative statement.

vocabulary.example: Je suis un cours du soir. — Moi aussi.
vocabulary.note: Reply used only after a positive statement.

vocabulary.example: Un conjoint peut accompagner le demandeur à l’entrevue.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; feminine `une conjointe`.

vocabulary.example: Un horaire de fin de semaine ne convient pas à tout le monde.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun despite its final -e.

practice.prompt: Reply agreeing: « Je n’ai pas encore reçu ma carte. » then « J’ai déjà pris rendez-vous. »
practice.hint: Opposite polarities require opposite particles.
practice.answer: Moi non plus. / Moi aussi.

takeaways: Positive equals `aussi`; negative equals `non plus`.
The stressed pronoun always comes first.
`Non plus` also adds a second excluded element.
keywords: agreeing with positive and negative statements

lessons.title: Les formes de la question
lessons.summary: French offers four question structures ranked by register: rising intonation and a final question word in conversation, `est-ce que` as the neutral choice, and inversion in formal speech and writing. With what, use `qu’est-ce qui` when the unknown element is the subject and `qu’est-ce que` when it is the object. `Quel` agrees with the noun it determines, and `n’est-ce pas` turns a statement into a confirmation question.
objectives: Select a question form that matches the register of the situation.
Distinguish subject and object questions with `what`.
Agree `quel` with the noun it introduces.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: Register is the level of formality suited to the audience. Rising intonation (`Vous avez un rendez-vous ?`) and a final question word (`Tu fais quoi ?`) belong to conversation. `Est-ce que` is neutral and safe everywhere. Inversion (`Que faites-vous ?`, `Avez-vous joint les pièces ?`) is the formal option and is expected in written questions.

The word for what depends on the grammatical role of the unknown element. If the missing element performs the verb, use `qu’est-ce qui`: `Qu’est-ce qui pourrait améliorer le transport public ?`. If it receives the action, use `qu’est-ce que` or the inverted `que`: `Qu’est-ce que vous proposez ?`, `Que proposez-vous ?`. For people, `qui` covers both roles: `Qui vous a reçu ?`, `Qui avez-vous rencontré ?`. `Quel` is a determiner and therefore agrees: `quel formulaire`, `quelle mesure`, `quels documents`, `quelles conditions`. Finally, `n’est-ce pas` at the end of a statement asks for confirmation.
points: Use intonation or a final question word only in informal speech.
Use `est-ce que` when you want a neutral, always-acceptable form.
Use inversion in formal speech and in written questions.
Choose `qu’est-ce qui` for an unknown subject and `qu’est-ce que` for an unknown object.
Agree `quel`, `quelle`, `quels`, `quelles` with the noun that follows.

examples.french: Qu’est-ce qui pourrait améliorer le transport public dans ce quartier ?
examples.english: What could improve public transit in this neighbourhood?
examples.note: The unknown element is the subject of « pourrait ».

examples.french: Qu’est-ce que vous proposez pour réduire les délais ?
examples.english: What do you propose in order to reduce processing times?
examples.note: The unknown element is the object of « proposez ».

examples.french: Quelles mesures proposez-vous pour protéger l’environnement ?
examples.english: What measures do you propose to protect the environment?
examples.note: « Quelles » agrees with the feminine plural noun, and the question uses inversion.

examples.french: Est-ce que le bureau est ouvert le samedi matin ?
examples.english: Is the office open on Saturday morning?
examples.note: Neutral form, suitable in every register.

examples.french: Vous avez joint les pièces justificatives, n’est-ce pas ?
examples.english: You attached the supporting documents, didn’t you?
examples.note: « N’est-ce pas » asks for confirmation.

mistakes.avoid: Qu’est-ce que se passe au guichet ?
mistakes.prefer: Qu’est-ce qui se passe au guichet ?
mistakes.why: The missing element is the subject of `se passe`, which requires `qui`.

mistakes.avoid: Quel mesures avez-vous prises ?
mistakes.prefer: Quelles mesures avez-vous prises ?
mistakes.why: `Quel` is a determiner and agrees with the feminine plural noun `mesures`.

vocabulary.example: Une réponse écrite est envoyée dans un délai de six semaines.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; `répondre à` is the related verb.

vocabulary.example: Une question précise obtient généralement une réponse plus utile.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; `poser une question` is the standard verb.

vocabulary.example: Est-ce que vous acceptez les documents numérisés ?
vocabulary.note: Neutral question opener; elides to `est-ce qu’` before a vowel.

vocabulary.example: Le dossier est complet, n’est-ce pas ?
vocabulary.note: Invariable tag placed at the end of a statement.

practice.prompt: Ask formally about the subject, then about the object: what is blocking the file, and what the office recommends.
practice.hint: One question uses `qu’est-ce qui`, the other can use inversion.
practice.answer: Qu’est-ce qui bloque le dossier ? Que recommande le bureau ?

takeaways: Intonation for speech, `est-ce que` for anything, inversion for formal writing.
Unknown subject equals `qu’est-ce qui`; unknown object equals `qu’est-ce que`.
`Quel` is a determiner and must agree.

modules.title: Le temps, le lieu et les prépositions
modules.description: Express locations, destinations, transport, durations, and relationships between words.

lessons.title: Les pays, les régions, les villes et l’origine
lessons.summary: With a city, use `à` for location and `de` for origin. With a feminine singular country, or a masculine one beginning with a vowel, use `en` and `de`: `en France`, `de France`, `en Iran`, `d’Iran`. With another masculine singular country, use `au` and `du`: `au Canada`, `du Canada`. With a plural country, use `aux` and `des`: `aux États-Unis`, `des États-Unis`. Countries ending in `-e` are usually feminine, but `le Mexique`, `le Cambodge`, `le Mozambique`, and `le Zimbabwe` are masculine.
objectives: Store each country name together with its article.
Derive the location and origin forms from gender, number, and initial sound.
Recall the four frequent masculine countries ending in `-e`.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: French treats place names in three groups. Cities normally take no article, so location is `à Montréal` and origin is `de Montréal`. Countries take an article, and that article drives everything: feminine singular gives `en` and `de`; masculine singular gives `au` and `du`; plural gives `aux` and `des`. A masculine country beginning with a vowel behaves like a feminine one for the sake of pronunciation: `en Iran`, `en Israël`.

The `-e` ending is a strong hint of a feminine country (`la France`, `la Suisse`, `la Belgique`, `la Roumanie`) but not a guarantee: `le Mexique`, `le Cambodge`, `le Mozambique`, and `le Zimbabwe` are masculine and take `au`. Canadian provinces follow the same logic as countries: `au Québec`, `en Ontario`, `en Colombie-Britannique`. Note also that `de` before a feminine country name usually appears without an article: `Je viens de France`, not `de la France`.
points: Learn the country with its article: `la France`, `le Canada`, `les États-Unis`.
Use `en` and `de` for a feminine country or a masculine one starting with a vowel.
Use `au` and `du` for other masculine countries.
Use `aux` and `des` for plural country names.
Memorise `le Mexique`, `le Cambodge`, `le Mozambique`, `le Zimbabwe` as masculine exceptions.

examples.french: J’habite au Canada et je travaille à Montréal.
examples.english: I live in Canada and work in Montreal.
examples.note: Masculine country with « au », city with « à ».

examples.french: Elle va en France pour poursuivre ses études de droit.
examples.english: She is going to France to continue her law studies.
examples.note: Feminine country with « en ».

examples.french: Je viens du Sénégal et ma collègue vient du Mexique.
examples.english: I come from Senegal and my colleague comes from Mexico.
examples.note: « Le Mexique » is masculine despite its -e ending.

examples.french: Ils sont revenus des États-Unis après une conférence de trois jours.
examples.english: They came back from the United States after a three-day conference.
examples.note: Plural country name with « des ».

examples.french: Nous nous sommes installés en Ontario avant de déménager au Québec.
examples.english: We settled in Ontario before moving to Quebec.
examples.note: Provinces follow the same rule as countries.

mistakes.avoid: Je vais au France pour trois semaines.
mistakes.prefer: Je vais en France pour trois semaines.
mistakes.why: `La France` is feminine, so location and destination take `en`.

mistakes.avoid: Elle arrive de le Mexique demain matin.
mistakes.prefer: Elle arrive du Mexique demain matin.
mistakes.why: `Le Mexique` is masculine, and `de + le` must contract to `du`.

vocabulary.example: La France accueille chaque année de nombreux étudiants étrangers.
vocabulary.note: Feminine country; `en France`, `de France`.

vocabulary.example: Le Mexique attire les voyageurs pour son patrimoine archéologique.
