takeaways: `On` is always singular, whatever it means.
Context decides between we, people, and someone.
`On` replaces an English passive; `nous` belongs to formal writing.

lessons.title: La différence entre « terminer » et « se terminer »
lessons.summary: `Terminer` is transitive: a person or an organisation completes something, so the verb needs a direct object. `Se terminer` is pronominal and takes the event itself as subject, with no agent named. The same pattern applies to several pairs: `commencer` and `se commencer` are rare together, but `ouvrir` and `s’ouvrir`, `fermer` and `se fermer`, `arrêter` and `s’arrêter` behave in the same way.
objectives: Decide whether an agent or the event itself is the subject.
Use `terminer` with a direct object and `se terminer` without one.
Transfer the pattern to comparable verb pairs.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: A transitive verb requires a direct object: someone finishes something. `Terminer` belongs to that group, so a French sentence with `terminer` must name what is being completed: `Je termine le rapport`, `L’équipe a terminé les corrections`. Leaving the object out makes the sentence incomplete.

The pronominal form removes the agent from view and puts the event in subject position: `La séance se termine à dix-sept heures`. Nobody is said to be ending the session; it simply comes to an end. The same contrast runs through several frequent pairs used in schedules and notices: `Le bureau ouvre à neuf heures` versus `La porte s’ouvre automatiquement`, `Le conducteur arrête le bus` versus `Le bus s’arrête devant la mairie`.
points: Name the object whenever you use `terminer`.
Use `se terminer` when the event is the subject and no agent is mentioned.
Choose `se terminer` for schedules, sessions, and deadlines.
Apply the same reasoning to `ouvrir` and `s’ouvrir`, `arrêter` and `s’arrêter`.
Remember that the pronominal form takes `être` in compound tenses.

examples.french: Je termine le rapport avant la réunion de quinze heures.
examples.english: I am finishing the report before the three o’clock meeting.
examples.note: Transitive use with a direct object.

examples.french: La séance se termine à dix-sept heures précises.
examples.english: The session ends at five o’clock sharp.
examples.note: The event itself is the subject.

examples.french: L’équipe a terminé les corrections, donc la formation s’est terminée plus tôt.
examples.english: The team finished the corrections, so the training ended earlier.
examples.note: Both forms in one sentence; the pronominal takes être.

examples.french: Le bus s’arrête devant la mairie, puis le conducteur arrête le moteur.
examples.english: The bus stops in front of the town hall, then the driver switches off the engine.
examples.note: The same contrast with « arrêter ».

examples.french: Le guichet ouvre à neuf heures et la porte s’ouvre automatiquement.
examples.english: The counter opens at nine o’clock and the door opens automatically.
examples.note: Agent implied for « ouvre », no agent for « s’ouvre ».

mistakes.avoid: La réunion termine à midi.
mistakes.prefer: La réunion se termine à midi.
mistakes.why: The event is the subject and no agent is named, so the pronominal form is required.

mistakes.avoid: Je me termine mon rapport ce soir.
mistakes.prefer: Je termine mon rapport ce soir.
mistakes.why: With an agent and a direct object, the verb is not pronominal.

vocabulary.example: Je termine la lettre de motivation avant la date limite.
vocabulary.note: Transitive: it always needs a direct object.

vocabulary.english: to end, to come to an end
vocabulary.example: La formation se termine par une évaluation écrite.
vocabulary.note: Pronominal; takes `être` in compound tenses.

vocabulary.example: Une séance d’information se termine toujours par une période de questions.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; `une séance` can also be a screening.

vocabulary.example: Un rapport détaillé résume les résultats de l’enquête.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; `faire un rapport` means to report.

practice.prompt: Choose the form: « L’atelier ___ à midi » and « Nous ___ l’atelier à midi ».
practice.hint: Only one sentence has an agent and an object.
practice.answer: L’atelier se termine à midi. Nous terminons l’atelier à midi.

takeaways: `Terminer` needs an object; `se terminer` needs none.
Schedules and sessions take the pronominal form.
The pattern extends to `s’ouvrir`, `se fermer`, `s’arrêter`.

lessons.title: Les constructions de « cacher » et de « rapporter »
lessons.summary: `Cacher quelque chose à quelqu’un` means to hide something from someone, so French uses `à` where English uses from. `Se cacher de quelqu’un` means to hide oneself from that person. `Rapporter` has three readings: to bring back, to report information, and to yield a return. `Se rapporter à` means to relate or refer to.
objectives: Use `à` after `cacher` where English would use from.
Distinguish the pronominal and non-pronominal forms.
Read `rapporter` correctly from its complement.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: The preposition belongs to the French verb, not to the English translation. `Cacher` is built as `cacher quelque chose à quelqu’un`, so `The company must not hide this information from employees` becomes `L’entreprise ne doit pas cacher cette information aux employés`. Adding the reflexive pronoun changes both the meaning and the preposition: `se cacher de quelqu’un` means to hide oneself from that person.

`Rapporter` is decided by its complement. With a concrete object it means to bring back: `Rapportez le formulaire signé`. With information it means to report: `Le témoin a rapporté les faits`. With money or an investment it means to yield: `Ce placement rapporte peu`. The pronominal `se rapporter à` is different again and means to relate to, typically used for a text, a statistic, or a rule: `Cette statistique se rapporte au marché du travail canadien`.
points: Build `cacher` as `cacher quelque chose à quelqu’un`.
Use `se cacher de quelqu’un` when the subject hides itself.
Read `rapporter` plus object as bring back.
Read `rapporter` plus information as report.
Use `se rapporter à` for a reference or a relationship between ideas.

examples.french: L’entreprise ne doit pas cacher cette information aux employés.
examples.english: The company must not hide this information from employees.
examples.note: French uses « à » where English uses from.

examples.french: Il se cachait de ses créanciers depuis plusieurs mois.
examples.english: He had been hiding from his creditors for several months.
examples.note: Pronominal form with « de ».

examples.french: Rapportez le formulaire signé au guichet avant seize heures.
examples.english: Bring the signed form back to the counter before four o’clock.
examples.note: « Rapporter » plus a concrete object.

examples.french: Le journal a rapporté les propos de la porte-parole sans les commenter.
examples.english: The newspaper reported the spokesperson’s words without commenting on them.
examples.note: « Rapporter » plus information.

examples.french: Cette statistique se rapporte au marché du travail canadien.
examples.english: This statistic relates to the Canadian labour market.
examples.note: « Se rapporter à » for a relationship between ideas.

mistakes.avoid: Il cache la vérité de ses collègues.
mistakes.prefer: Il cache la vérité à ses collègues.
mistakes.why: `Cacher quelque chose à quelqu’un` uses `à`, even though English uses from.

mistakes.avoid: Ce chapitre rapporte à la question du logement.
mistakes.prefer: Ce chapitre se rapporte à la question du logement.
mistakes.why: In the sense of relating to, the verb is pronominal: `se rapporter à`.

vocabulary.example: Elle n’a rien caché à son employeur au sujet de son horaire.
vocabulary.note: The person is introduced by `à`, never by `de`.

vocabulary.english: to relate to, to refer to
vocabulary.example: Ce paragraphe se rapporte aux conditions d’admission.
vocabulary.note: Pronominal; the complement is introduced by `à`.

vocabulary.example: Un employé à temps partiel a droit aux mêmes protections.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; feminine `une employée`.

vocabulary.example: Une statistique récente montre une hausse du nombre de demandes.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; usually plural when it names the discipline.

practice.prompt: Translate: « She did not hide the delay from the committee, and this note refers to the same file. »
practice.hint: One `à` after `cacher`, one pronominal verb.
practice.answer: Elle n’a pas caché le retard au comité, et cette note se rapporte au même dossier.

takeaways: `Cacher quelque chose à quelqu’un`, not `de`.
`Se cacher de` for hiding oneself.
`Se rapporter à` equals to relate to.
keywords: cacher, se cacher, rapporter, and se rapporter

lessons.title: Le verbe « aller à » au sens de « convenir »
lessons.summary: Besides movement, `aller à` means to suit someone. The item that suits is the grammatical subject and the person is an indirect object: `Cette veste va bien à la candidate`, `Cette coupe de cheveux me va bien`. The adverbs `bien`, `très bien`, and `mal` grade the judgement. A related expression, `aller avec`, says that two items match each other.
objectives: Put the item, not the person, in subject position.
Use an indirect pronoun for the person concerned.
Separate this meaning from movement and from `aller avec`.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: In this construction the roles are the reverse of English. The clothing, the colour, or the hairstyle is the subject, and the person is an indirect object introduced by `à` or replaced by `me`, `te`, `lui`, `nous`, `vous`, `leur`. English says She suits that jacket only rarely; French always says `Cette veste lui va bien`.

Two neighbouring expressions are worth keeping apart. `Aller avec` links two items rather than an item and a person: `Cette cravate va bien avec la chemise bleue`. And ordinary movement remains available with the same verb, so the context decides: `Elle va à l’entrevue` is movement, `Cette veste lui va` is suitability. The adverb usually accompanies the judgement: `bien`, `très bien`, `mal`, `parfaitement`.
points: Make the item that suits the grammatical subject.
Introduce the person with `à` or with an indirect pronoun.
Add `bien`, `très bien`, or `mal` to grade the judgement.
Use `aller avec` when two items match each other.
Rely on the context to separate this meaning from movement.

examples.french: Cette veste sobre va bien à la candidate.
examples.english: This understated jacket suits the candidate.
examples.note: The item is the subject; the person follows « à ».

examples.french: Cette coupe de cheveux me va bien pour une entrevue.
examples.english: This haircut suits me well for an interview.
examples.note: The person is an indirect pronoun placed before the verb.

examples.french: Le rose pâle lui va très bien, mais le vert foncé lui va mal.
examples.english: Pale pink suits her very well, but dark green does not suit her at all.
examples.note: Adverbs grade the judgement.

examples.french: Cette cravate va bien avec la chemise bleue.
examples.english: This tie goes well with the blue shirt.
examples.note: « Aller avec » links two items.

examples.french: Elle va à l’entrevue en tailleur, parce que ce vêtement lui va bien.
examples.english: She is going to the interview in a suit, because that outfit suits her.
examples.note: Movement and suitability in the same sentence.

mistakes.avoid: Elle va bien cette veste pour l’entrevue.
mistakes.prefer: Cette veste lui va bien pour l’entrevue.
mistakes.why: The item that suits is the subject and the person is an indirect object.

mistakes.avoid: Cette cravate va bien à la chemise bleue.
mistakes.prefer: Cette cravate va bien avec la chemise bleue.
mistakes.why: Two items are matched with `aller avec`; `aller à` is reserved for a person.

vocabulary.example: Ce manteau vous va très bien.
vocabulary.note: The person is an indirect object; distinct from `aller avec` for two items.

vocabulary.example: Une veste sobre convient à un entretien d’embauche.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; `un veston` is used in Canada for a suit jacket.

vocabulary.example: Une coupe de cheveux nette donne une impression soignée.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun phrase; the gender comes from `coupe`.

vocabulary.example: Le rose pâle va particulièrement bien avec une chemise blanche.
vocabulary.note: Masculine when it names the colour, unlike the flower `une rose`.

practice.prompt: Translate: « This colour suits you, and it goes well with your jacket. »
practice.hint: One indirect pronoun, then `aller avec`.
practice.answer: Cette couleur vous va bien, et elle va bien avec votre veste.

takeaways: The item is the subject, the person is indirect.
`Bien`, `très bien`, `mal` grade the judgement.
`Aller avec` matches two items; `aller à` matches an item to a person.

modules.title: Le vocabulaire du quotidien
modules.description: Use practical vocabulary for daily life, health, food, weather, travel, and culture.

lessons.title: La météo et les moments de la journée
lessons.summary: Weather is impersonal in French: the subject `il` refers to nothing. Use `il fait` plus an adjective for a general condition (`il fait froid`), `il y a` plus a weather noun for a phenomenon (`il y a du vent`, `il y a du verglas`), and `le temps est` plus an adjective for a description (`le temps est nuageux`). For times of day, `le soir` is the recurring part of the day, `une soirée` an evening as an event or a span, and `la nuit` the night-time period.
objectives: Choose the right impersonal frame before naming the weather.
Use a weather noun with `il y a` and an adjective with `il fait`.
Separate `le soir`, `une soirée`, and `la nuit`.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: An impersonal construction has a grammatical subject that refers to nothing at all. French weather works that way: `il` in `il fait froid` is not a person. Choose the frame first, then insert the word. `Il fait` is followed by an adjective or a bare noun of temperature: `il fait beau`, `il fait mauvais`, `il fait froid`, `il fait chaud`, `il fait moins dix`. `Il y a` is followed by a weather noun with its article: `il y a du vent`, `il y a de la pluie`, `il y a du verglas`. `Le temps est` is followed by a descriptive adjective: `le temps est ensoleillé`, `le temps est nuageux`.

The parts of the day are distinguished by their aspect. `Le soir` names the recurring period and is used adverbially: `Le soir, nous écoutons la radio`. `Une soirée` presents the evening as an event or as a measured span, which is why greetings use it: `Passez une bonne soirée`. `La nuit` covers the night-time hours. The same pair exists for `le jour` and `une journée`, `le matin` and `une matinée`, `l’an` and `une année`.
points: Use `il fait` plus adjective for the general feel of the weather.
Use `il y a` plus an article and a weather noun for a phenomenon.
Use `le temps est` plus adjective for a descriptive report.
Use `le soir` for the recurring period and `une soirée` for the event.
Apply the same contrast to `jour` and `journée`, `matin` and `matinée`.

examples.french: Il fait froid ce matin, mais le temps est ensoleillé.
examples.english: It is cold this morning, but the weather is sunny.
examples.note: Two different frames in one sentence.

examples.french: Il y avait du verglas toute la matinée, alors les autobus étaient en retard.
examples.english: There was black ice all morning, so the buses were late.
examples.note: « Il y a » plus a weather noun; « verglas » is ice on the ground, not freezing rain.

examples.french: Il y a du vent et de la pluie depuis hier soir.
examples.english: It has been windy and rainy since yesterday evening.
examples.note: Weather nouns keep their partitive article.

examples.french: J’ai assisté à une activité culturelle hier soir.
examples.english: I attended a cultural event last night.
examples.note: « Hier soir » uses the recurring period word.

examples.french: Passez une bonne soirée après la cérémonie d’accueil !
examples.english: Have a good evening after the welcome ceremony!
examples.note: « Soirée » presents the evening as an event.

mistakes.avoid: Il fait du vent et il y a froid aujourd’hui.
mistakes.prefer: Il y a du vent et il fait froid aujourd’hui.
mistakes.why: A weather noun goes with `il y a`, and an adjective goes with `il fait`.

mistakes.avoid: Bonne soir et à demain !
mistakes.prefer: Bonne soirée et à demain !
mistakes.why: A greeting presents the evening as a span, which requires `soirée`.

vocabulary.example: Le verglas rend les trottoirs dangereux en février.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; freezing rain is `la pluie verglaçante`.

vocabulary.example: Une soirée conviviale a réuni tous les nouveaux voisins.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; `le soir` names the recurring period instead.

vocabulary.example: Le vent du nord a fait tomber plusieurs branches.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; used with `il y a du vent`.

vocabulary.example: La pluie fine a commencé pendant notre promenade.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; used with `il y a de la pluie`.

vocabulary.example: Une matinée entière a été consacrée aux entrevues.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; `le matin` names the recurring period.

practice.prompt: Say in French: it is hot today, there is fog, and the weather is cloudy.
practice.hint: Three different frames.
practice.answer: Il fait chaud aujourd’hui, il y a du brouillard et le temps est nuageux.

takeaways: Adjective goes with `il fait`; weather noun goes with `il y a`.
`Le temps est` introduces a descriptive adjective.
`Le soir` recurs; `une soirée` is an event.
keywords: weather and parts of the day

lessons.title: Le corps, la douleur, les odeurs et les sensations
lessons.summary: Pain uses `avoir mal à` plus a definite article, contracted where required: `j’ai mal à la tête`, `au dos`, `aux dents`. `Avoir mal au cœur` is idiomatic and means to feel nauseous, not to have a heart problem. `Sentir` covers giving off a smell and perceiving physically; `se sentir` reports how a person feels. `Faire mal à` names who is hurting: `Le dos me fait mal`.
objectives: Build `avoir mal à` with the correct contracted article.
Separate `sentir`, `se sentir`, and `faire mal`.
Interpret `avoir mal au cœur` correctly.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: With `avoir mal à`, the body part takes a definite article, never a possessive, because the subject already identifies the owner: `J’ai mal à la tête`, `Il a mal au dos`, `Elle a mal aux dents`. The contraction rules apply exactly as elsewhere: `à + le` gives `au`, `à + les` gives `aux`. An alternative structure reverses the roles: `Le dos me fait mal`, where the body part is the subject and the person is an indirect pronoun.

Three verbs must be kept apart. `Sentir` with a direct object means to smell or to perceive something: `Je ne sens rien dans la main gauche`. `Sentir` with an adjective or a noun means to give off a smell: `Ce plat sent très bon`, `La salle sent la peinture`. `Se sentir` plus an adjective reports a state: `Comment est-ce que vous vous sentez ?`. Finally, `avoir mal au cœur` is an idiom meaning to feel sick or nauseous; a heart condition would be `un problème cardiaque`.
points: Use `avoir mal à` plus the definite article of the body part.
Contract to `au` and `aux` where the gender and number require it.
Use `faire mal à` when the body part is the subject.
Use `sentir` for smelling or perceiving, `se sentir` for a personal state.
Read `avoir mal au cœur` as nausea.

examples.french: J’ai mal à la tête depuis le début de mon quart de travail.
examples.english: I have had a headache since the start of my shift.
examples.note: Definite article, no possessive.

examples.french: Il a mal au dos et aux épaules après cette journée de déménagement.
examples.english: His back and shoulders hurt after this day of moving.
examples.note: Contractions « au » and « aux ».

examples.french: Comment est-ce que vous vous sentez depuis votre traitement ?
examples.english: How have you been feeling since your treatment?
examples.note: « Se sentir » reports a personal state.

examples.french: Je ne sens rien dans la main gauche depuis l’accident.
examples.english: I cannot feel anything in my left hand since the accident.
examples.note: « Sentir » in its perception meaning.

examples.french: Ce plat sent très bon, mais j’ai mal au cœur depuis ce matin.
examples.english: This dish smells very good, but I have been feeling sick since this morning.
examples.note: « Sentir » for a smell, and the idiom « avoir mal au cœur ».

mistakes.avoid: J’ai mal à mon dos depuis hier.
mistakes.prefer: J’ai mal au dos depuis hier.
mistakes.why: French uses the definite article with a body part in this construction, and `à + le` contracts.

mistakes.avoid: Je sens fatigué après cette journée.
mistakes.prefer: Je me sens fatigué après cette journée.
mistakes.why: Reporting one’s own state requires the pronominal `se sentir`.

vocabulary.example: La tête du patient reste immobile pendant l’examen.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; `avoir mal à la tête` means to have a headache.

vocabulary.example: Le dos me fait mal après une longue journée debout.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; contracts to `au dos` after `avoir mal à`.

vocabulary.example: Je me sens beaucoup mieux depuis le début du traitement.
vocabulary.note: Pronominal; followed by an adjective or an adverb.

vocabulary.example: Un quart de travail de nuit demande une bonne organisation du sommeil.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun phrase used in Canada; `un poste` is used in France.

vocabulary.example: Un traitement de six semaines a été prescrit par la clinique.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; the ending -ment is a masculine hint.

practice.prompt: Say in French: my teeth hurt, I feel tired, and this room smells of paint.
practice.hint: Three different structures, one of them with a contraction.
practice.answer: J’ai mal aux dents, je me sens fatigué et cette salle sent la peinture.

takeaways: `Avoir mal à` plus a definite article, contracted as needed.
`Sentir` perceives or gives off a smell; `se sentir` reports a state.
`Avoir mal au cœur` equals nausea.
keywords: the body, pain, smell, and feeling

lessons.title: Les sports, les activités et les instruments
lessons.summary: Use `jouer à` for a game or a sport with rules (`jouer au tennis`, `jouer aux cartes`), `jouer de` for a musical instrument (`jouer de la guitare`, `jouer du piano`), and `faire de` for an activity practised regularly (`faire de la natation`, `faire du ski`). The article contracts with the preposition, so `à + le` gives `au` and `de + le` gives `du`.
objectives: Match each activity type with its preposition.
Contract the article correctly inside the expression.
Choose between `jouer de` and `faire de` for music.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: The preposition encodes the type of activity, so the choice is lexical rather than logical. Games and sports with an opponent or rules take `jouer à`: `jouer au soccer`, `jouer au hockey`, `jouer aux échecs`. Musical instruments take `jouer de`: `jouer de la guitare`, `jouer du violon`, `jouer de la batterie`. Activities practised as a discipline take `faire de`: `faire de la natation`, `faire du vélo`, `faire de la randonnée`.

The article is part of the expression and contracts normally, which is why the same sport can appear as `au`, `à la`, or `aux` depending on its gender and number. `Faire de` is also possible with a sport (`faire du tennis`) and then presents it as a regular practice rather than as a match being played. For music, `faire de la musique` describes the activity in general, while `jouer de` names the instrument.
points: Use `jouer à` for games and sports with rules.
Use `jouer de` for a musical instrument.
Use `faire de` for an activity practised regularly.
Contract the article: `au tennis`, `du piano`, `aux cartes`.
Use `faire de la musique` for the general activity and `jouer de` for the instrument.

examples.french: Il joue au tennis au centre communautaire deux fois par semaine.
examples.english: He plays tennis at the community centre twice a week.
examples.note: « Jouer à » plus a contracted article.

examples.french: Je joue de la guitare pendant le festival francophone.
examples.english: I play the guitar during the Francophone festival.
examples.note: « Jouer de » for an instrument.

examples.french: Je fais du ski de fond chaque hiver dans le parc régional.
examples.english: I go cross-country skiing every winter in the regional park.
examples.note: « Faire de » for a regular activity.

examples.french: Ma fille joue aux échecs et fait de la natation le samedi.
examples.english: My daughter plays chess and swims on Saturdays.
examples.note: « Aux » for a plural game, « de la » for an activity.

examples.french: Il fait de la musique depuis dix ans et joue du piano à la chorale.
examples.english: He has been making music for ten years and plays the piano in the choir.
examples.note: « Faire de la musique » in general, « jouer du piano » for the instrument.

mistakes.avoid: Elle joue le piano depuis trois ans.
mistakes.prefer: Elle joue du piano depuis trois ans.
mistakes.why: An instrument requires `jouer de`, with the article contracted.

mistakes.avoid: Nous jouons à la natation le mardi.
mistakes.prefer: Nous faisons de la natation le mardi.
mistakes.why: Swimming is a practised activity, so it takes `faire de`.

vocabulary.example: Le tennis demande de la précision et une bonne endurance.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; `jouer au tennis`.

vocabulary.example: La guitare acoustique accompagne doucement la chanteuse.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; `jouer de la guitare`.

vocabulary.example: La natation est proposée gratuitement à la piscine municipale.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; `faire de la natation`.

vocabulary.example: Une chorale de quartier répète dans la salle municipale.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun; the singer is `un choriste`.

practice.prompt: Complete: « Il joue ___ hockey, elle joue ___ violon et nous faisons ___ randonnée. »
practice.hint: Sport, instrument, activity.
practice.answer: Il joue au hockey, elle joue du violon et nous faisons de la randonnée.

takeaways: Game equals `jouer à`; instrument equals `jouer de`; activity equals `faire de`.
The article always contracts inside the expression.
`Faire du tennis` presents the sport as a practice, `jouer au tennis` as a match.

lessons.title: La nourriture, les quantités et les portions
lessons.summary: Use a partitive article for an unmeasured amount of food: `du pain`, `de la farine`, `des légumes`. As soon as the quantity is measured, the article disappears and only `de` remains: `un kilo de pommes`, `beaucoup de pain`, `une tranche de fromage`. `La moitié de` names half of a specific whole, and a definite article expresses a rate: `trois dollars le kilo`.
objectives: Use partitive articles for unmeasured food.
Drop the article after any expression of quantity.
Express a unit price with a definite article.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: A partitive article presents an unmeasured portion of something uncountable: `du lait`, `de la farine`, `de l’eau`, and the plural `des légumes`. It answers the question some what, and English usually leaves it out, which is why it is easy to forget: `Je prends du café` is I have coffee, not I have the coffee.

The moment a quantity is stated, the article vanishes and only `de` remains. That applies to weights and containers (`un kilo de pommes`, `une bouteille d’eau`, `une tranche de pain`), to adverbs of quantity (`beaucoup de légumes`, `peu de sel`, `assez de temps`), and after a negation (`Je n’ai pas de pain`). Two related structures complete the topic: `la moitié de` for half of a specific whole (`la moitié des repas`), and the definite article for a unit price (`trois dollars le kilo`, `deux dollars la pièce`).
points: Use `du`, `de la`, `de l’`, `des` for an unspecified amount.
Reduce to `de` alone after a weight, a container, or an adverb of quantity.
Reduce to `de` alone after a negation.
Use `la moitié de` plus a determined noun for half of a specific whole.
Use `le`, `la`, or `les` before the unit when giving a rate.

examples.french: La banque alimentaire distribue du lait, de la farine et des légumes frais.
examples.english: The food bank distributes milk, flour, and fresh vegetables.
examples.note: Three partitive forms for unmeasured amounts.

examples.french: J’ai acheté un kilo de pommes et beaucoup de légumes au marché.
examples.english: I bought a kilo of apples and a lot of vegetables at the market.
examples.note: After a quantity, only « de » remains.

examples.french: Le centre communautaire a gardé la moitié des repas pour les bénévoles.
examples.english: The community centre kept half of the meals for the volunteers.
examples.note: « La moitié de » plus a determined noun.

examples.french: Les pommes locales coûtent trois dollars le kilo cette semaine.
examples.english: Local apples cost three dollars per kilo this week.
examples.note: The definite article expresses a rate.

examples.french: Il n’y a plus de café, mais il reste de la soupe et du pain.
examples.english: There is no coffee left, but there is still soup and bread.
examples.note: Negation reduces to « de »; the positive clause keeps the partitive.

mistakes.avoid: J’ai acheté beaucoup des légumes au marché.
mistakes.prefer: J’ai acheté beaucoup de légumes au marché.
mistakes.why: An adverb of quantity is followed by `de` alone, without an article.

mistakes.avoid: Je voudrais le pain et la confiture, s’il vous plaît.
mistakes.prefer: Je voudrais du pain et de la confiture, s’il vous plaît.
mistakes.why: An unmeasured amount takes a partitive article, not a definite one.

vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; `du pain` for an unspecified amount.

vocabulary.example: La confiture de fraises est préparée avec les fruits du jardin.

vocabulary.note: Feminine noun phrase; the gender comes from `banque`.

practice.hint: Partitive, quantity, partitive, negation.
practice.answer: Je voudrais de l’eau, un litre de lait et des pommes ; il n’y a plus de sucre.

takeaways: Unmeasured food takes `du`, `de la`, `de l’`, `des`.
Any stated quantity or a negation reduces the article to `de`.
A rate uses the definite article: `trois dollars le kilo`.

lessons.title: La maison, les voyages et les services
lessons.summary: Everyday service situations rely on fixed phrases that are faster to reuse than to build word by word: `Où se trouve…, s’il vous plaît ?`, `au rez-de-chaussée`, `au premier étage`, `au fond du couloir`, `réserver une voiture de location`, `faire les courses`. Note that `faire les courses` means grocery shopping, while leisure shopping is `faire du shopping` or `faire les magasins`.
objectives: Ask where a service is located in a polite, ready-made form.
Understand floor and direction indications.
Separate grocery shopping from leisure shopping.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: A lexical chunk is a multiword expression stored and reused as a unit. In service situations, chunks save processing time and sound more natural than assembled sentences. The core request is `Pardon, où se trouve le bureau d’accueil, s’il vous plaît ?`, and its variants use the same frame: `Où se trouvent les toilettes ?`, `Où est-ce que je peux payer ?`.

Floor indications differ from English. `Le rez-de-chaussée` is the ground floor, and `le premier étage` is the floor above it, so English first floor and French `premier étage` are not the same level. Directions reuse the spatial phrases: `au fond du couloir`, `au bout du corridor`, `en face de l’ascenseur`, `à droite`, `à gauche`. Finally, two shopping expressions must be kept apart: `faire les courses` is buying groceries and necessities, while `faire du shopping` or `faire les magasins` is browsing for pleasure.
points: Open a request with `Pardon` and close it with `s’il vous plaît`.
Use `Où se trouve` plus a singular noun and `Où se trouvent` plus a plural.
Read `le rez-de-chaussée` as the ground floor and `le premier étage` as the one above.
Reuse the direction chunks: `au fond de`, `en face de`, `à droite`, `à gauche`.
Use `faire les courses` for groceries and `faire du shopping` for leisure.

examples.french: Pardon, où se trouve le bureau d’accueil, s’il vous plaît ?
examples.english: Excuse me, where is the reception desk, please?
examples.note: The standard polite request frame.

examples.french: Le bureau d’accueil est au rez-de-chaussée de l’hôtel de ville.
examples.english: The reception desk is on the ground floor of city hall.
examples.note: « Rez-de-chaussée » is the ground floor, not the first floor.

examples.french: Le service des permis est au premier étage, au fond du couloir.
examples.english: The permits office is one floor up, at the end of the corridor.
examples.note: Two chunks combined in a direction.

examples.french: Nous devons réserver une voiture de location pour visiter la région.
examples.english: We need to book a rental car to visit the region.
examples.note: Fixed expression for renting a vehicle.

examples.french: Nous finissons notre dîner avant d’aller faire les courses.
examples.english: We finish lunch before going grocery shopping.
examples.note: In Canada « le dîner » is the midday meal; « faire les courses » is grocery shopping.

mistakes.avoid: Pardon, où se trouvent le bureau d’accueil, s’il vous plaît ?
mistakes.prefer: Pardon, où se trouve le bureau d’accueil, s’il vous plaît ?
mistakes.why: `Se trouver` agrees with its subject; `le bureau d’accueil` is singular, so the verb stays singular.

mistakes.avoid: Je vais faire du shopping : il me faut du lait et du pain.
mistakes.prefer: Je vais faire les courses : il me faut du lait et du pain.
mistakes.why: Buying groceries is `faire les courses`; `faire du shopping` refers to leisure shopping.

vocabulary.note: Masculine compound; `l’accueil` alone also means reception.

vocabulary.example: Le rez-de-chaussée abrite la réception et la salle d’attente.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; invariable in the plural.

vocabulary.example: Une voiture de location nous permettra d’explorer la région.
vocabulary.note: Feminine noun phrase; the gender comes from `voiture`.

vocabulary.example: Nous faisons les courses le samedi matin au marché du quartier.
vocabulary.note: Distinct from `faire du shopping`, which is leisure shopping.

vocabulary.example: Un arrêt d’autobus se trouve juste devant l’immeuble.
vocabulary.note: Masculine compound; `un arrêt de bus` is the usual form in France.

practice.prompt: Ask politely where the permits office is, then say it is on the first floor above the ground floor.
practice.hint: Use the request frame and the French floor word.
practice.answer: Pardon, où se trouve le service des permis, s’il vous plaît ? Il est au premier étage.

takeaways: `Pardon, où se trouve…, s’il vous plaît ?` is the reusable request.
`Rez-de-chaussée` equals ground floor; `premier étage` is above it.
`Faire les courses` equals groceries, not leisure shopping.

lessons.title: Les échanges et les réactions idiomatiques
lessons.summary: Conversational chunks resist word-by-word translation and carry a register. `Ça va` covers both wellbeing and agreement; `ça y est` marks completion; `ça ne fait rien` dismisses a problem; `vas-y` and `allez-y` mean go ahead; `tenez` and `tiens` accompany handing something over; `le plaisir est partagé` returns a compliment. `Occupe-toi de tes oignons` is informal and belongs only to conversation between peers.
objectives: Use the frequent `ça` reactions accurately.
Choose a chunk that matches the formality of the situation.
Recognise informal expressions without reusing them in writing.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: Register is the level of formality suited to the audience. Several of these chunks are built on `ça`, which is itself informal but entirely normal in speech. `Ça va` asks or reports wellbeing (`Ça va ? — Ça va, merci`) and also signals that something is acceptable (`Ça va comme ça`). `Ça y est` announces that something is finally done. `Ça ne fait rien` and its slightly more formal variant `cela ne fait rien` dismiss an apology.

A second group accompanies actions. `Vas-y` and the polite `allez-y` mean go ahead, both as encouragement and as permission. `Tiens` and `tenez` accompany handing something over, close to English here you go. To return a compliment after `Enchanté` or `C’était un plaisir`, French says `Le plaisir est partagé` or `Tout le plaisir est pour moi`. Finally, `occupe-toi de tes oignons` means mind your own business: it is useful to recognise but too familiar for an exam text or any formal exchange.
points: Use `Ça va ?` to ask about someone and `Ça va` to answer.
Use `ça y est` only when the action is now complete.
Use `ça ne fait rien` to dismiss an apology or a small problem.
Use `tenez` with `vous` and `tiens` with `tu` when handing something over.
Keep `occupe-toi de tes oignons` for informal speech among peers.

examples.french: — Ça va ? — Ça va, merci. Tenez, voici votre reçu.
examples.english: “How are you?” “I’m fine, thanks. Here, this is your receipt.”
examples.note: Two everyday chunks in a service exchange.

examples.french: Ça y est, j’ai fini de remplir le dossier en ligne !
examples.english: That’s it, I have finished filling in the file online!
examples.note: « Ça y est » marks completion.

examples.french: Je suis désolé pour le retard. — Cela ne fait rien.
examples.english: I am sorry about the delay. — It does not matter.
examples.note: Slightly more formal variant of « ça ne fait rien ».

examples.french: Vous pouvez poser votre question. — Allez-y, je vous écoute.
examples.english: You can ask your question. — Go ahead, I am listening.
examples.note: Polite form of « vas-y ».

examples.french: Merci pour cette conversation. — Le plaisir est partagé.
examples.english: Thank you for this conversation. — The pleasure is mutual.
examples.note: Standard way of returning a compliment.

mistakes.avoid: Merci beaucoup. — Plaisir partagé.
mistakes.prefer: Merci beaucoup. — Le plaisir est partagé.
mistakes.why: The expression requires the full clause; the bare noun phrase is not idiomatic.

mistakes.avoid: Ça fait rien, je vais attendre le prochain rendez-vous.
mistakes.prefer: Cela ne fait rien, je vais attendre le prochain rendez-vous.
mistakes.why: Dropping `ne` and using `ça` are normal in speech, but a written or formal exchange keeps `ne` and prefers `cela`.

vocabulary.example: Ça y est, le formulaire est envoyé et confirmé.
vocabulary.note: Marks completion; informal but very frequent.

vocabulary.example: Vous êtes en retard de cinq minutes ? Ça ne fait rien.
vocabulary.note: `Cela ne fait rien` is the slightly more formal variant.

vocabulary.example: Merci de votre accueil. — Le plaisir est partagé.
vocabulary.note: Full clause; `plaisir partagé` alone is not idiomatic.

vocabulary.example: Un reçu officiel est remis après chaque paiement.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun, from the past participle of `recevoir`.

practice.prompt: Complete the exchange: « — ___ ? — ___, merci. ___, voici votre attestation. »
practice.hint: Greeting, reply, and handing something over politely.
practice.answer: — Ça va ? — Ça va, merci. Tenez, voici votre attestation.

takeaways: `Ça va`, `ça y est`, `ça ne fait rien` cover most everyday reactions.
`Tenez` with `vous`, `tiens` with `tu`.
Recognise very familiar idioms, but keep them out of formal writing.

lessons.title: Les pays et les nationalités
lessons.summary: Learn each country with its article and connect it to three related forms: the masculine adjective, the feminine adjective, and the capitalised noun for a person. Most feminine adjectives simply add `-e` (`allemand` gives `allemande`), several double the consonant (`canadien` gives `canadienne`), and some are identical in both genders (`belge`, `russe`, `suisse`).
objectives: Store a country, its adjective, and its person noun as one set.
Form the feminine adjective, including the doubled-consonant group.
Apply the capitalisation rule consistently.

sections.title: Core concept
paragraphs: Each country gives a small family of words. `L’Allemagne` gives `allemand`, `allemande`, and `un Allemand` or `une Allemande`; `le Canada` gives `canadien`, `canadienne`, and `un Canadien` or `une Canadienne`. Building the set once is far more efficient than meeting each form separately, and it also fixes the gender of the country name.

Three feminine patterns cover most cases. Simple addition of `-e`: `allemand` gives `allemande`, `français` gives `française`. Doubling before `-e`: `canadien` gives `canadienne`, `italien` gives `italienne`. No change at all when the masculine already ends in `-e`: `belge`, `russe`, `suisse`, `roumain` being the exception that follows the first pattern. Capitalisation depends on function: lowercase for the adjective and for the language, capital for the noun naming a person.
points: Record the country with its article, then both adjective forms, then the person noun.
Add `-e` for most feminine adjectives.
Double the final consonant in the `-ien` and `-éen` groups.
Leave adjectives already ending in `-e` unchanged.
Capitalise only the noun that names a person.

examples.english: She is Canadian and works for a settlement support organisation.
examples.note: Lowercase adjective after « être ».

examples.french: C’est un Britannique installé au Québec depuis dix ans.
examples.english: He is a British man who has lived in Quebec for ten years.
examples.note: Capitalised noun naming a person.

examples.french: L’Allemagne compte seize Länder et partage une frontière avec la France.
examples.english: Germany has sixteen states and shares a border with France.
examples.note: Feminine country with its article.

examples.french: Une étudiante roumaine et un collègue russe ont présenté le projet.
examples.english: A Romanian student and a Russian colleague presented the project.
examples.note: « Roumaine » adds -e; « russe » is identical in both genders.

examples.french: Le Royaume-Uni réunit quatre nations et reste un partenaire commercial important.
examples.english: The United Kingdom brings together four nations and remains an important trading partner.
examples.note: Masculine country name with a compound form.

mistakes.avoid: Elle est Canadienne et elle parle Anglais.
mistakes.prefer: Elle est canadienne et elle parle anglais.
mistakes.why: After `être` the word is an adjective, and a language name is always lowercase.

mistakes.avoid: J’ai rencontré une italien pendant la formation.
mistakes.prefer: J’ai rencontré une Italienne pendant la formation.
mistakes.why: The noun naming a person is capitalised and agrees in gender.

vocabulary.example: L’Allemagne accueille chaque année de nombreux travailleurs qualifiés.
vocabulary.note: Feminine country; adjective `allemand`, `allemande`.

vocabulary.example: Le Royaume-Uni réunit quatre nations.
vocabulary.note: Masculine country; the adjective is `britannique` for both genders.

vocabulary.example: La Roumanie possède de nombreuses régions montagneuses.
vocabulary.note: Feminine country; adjective `roumain`, `roumaine`.

vocabulary.example: Une entreprise canadienne a financé une partie du projet.
vocabulary.note: The feminine doubles the final consonant before -e.

vocabulary.example: Un organisme communautaire accompagne les familles nouvellement arrivées.
vocabulary.note: Masculine noun; the ending -isme is a masculine hint.
